Surat al-An'am (Chapter of the Cattle) is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority, and it was said that it was revealed all at once.

Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: It is Meccan except for two verses that were revealed in Medina. The first is ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ [al-An'am 6:91], which was revealed concerning the two Jews Malik ibn al-Sayf and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. The second is ﴿It is He who brought into being gardens, both trellised and untrellised﴾ [al-An'am 6:141], which was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas.

Ibn Jurayj said: It was revealed concerning Mu'adh ibn Jabal. It was also said: Seventy thousand angels escorted this surah.

﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light. Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾ ﴿It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him. Yet you still doubt.﴾ ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth. He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn.﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾, to the end of the verse. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The opening of the Torah is the opening of al-An'am up to His saying ﴿ascribe equals﴾, and the closing of the Torah is the closing of Hud.

His saying ﴿Praise belongs to God﴾ is in the form of a declarative statement, but it carries the meaning of a command. This is preferable to phrasing it as a command, saying "Praise God," for two reasons. First, it includes teaching both the wording and the meaning, whereas a command conveys only the meaning and not the wording. Second, proof (burhan) testifies only to the meaning of a declarative statement, not to that of a command.

﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾: The creation of the heavens and the earth are blessings that deserve praise, for the earth bears and the sky shades. They are among the first of His blessings upon His creation. For this reason He sought praise by means of their creation, and He attributed their creation to Himself when calling for praise, so that the one deserving praise is the Creator of the heavens and the earth. Thus He alone is deserving of praise, since He alone created the heavens and the earth.

Regarding the plural "heavens" and the singular "earth," there are two explanations. First, the heavens are nobler than the earth, and the plural is more emphatic than the singular, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr 15:9]. Second, His commands to the earth pass through all seven heavens.

Regarding the placing of the heavens before the earth, there are two explanations. First, because their creation preceded that of the earth. Second, because of their nobility, He placed them before the earth in mention, even though they were created after the earth.

These two explanations reflect the scholars' disagreement over which of the two was created first.

﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾: meaning "and created." He varied the wording so that the structure would be more elegant (nazm, the arrangement of the text). Regarding "the darknesses and the light" here, there are three explanations. The first, which is the well-known view from Qatadah, is that He mentioned darkness before light because He mentioned the creation of darkness before the creation of light. He used the plural "darknesses" and the singular "light" because darkness is more general than light.

The second: the darknesses are the night, and the light is the day.

The third: the darknesses are disbelief, and the light is faith. This was said by al-Suddi.

The people of the khawatir (inward inspirations, a term of Sufi and speculative writers) have three further explanations:

The first: the darknesses are bodies, and the light is spirits.

The second: the darknesses are the deeds of the bodies, and the light is the inner intentions of the hearts.

The third: the darknesses are ignorance, and the light is knowledge.

﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾: that is, they make for Him, alongside these blessings, an equal (adl), meaning a like.

Regarding this there are two views. The first is that they ascribe to Him the idols they worship. The second is that they ascribe to Him another god who did not create the like of His creation.

﴿It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him﴾: Regarding these two terms, there are four views. The first is that the first term He decreed is the term of life until death, and the second specified term with Him is the term from death until resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: the first term He decreed is the term of this world, and the second term, specified "from Him," is the beginning of the Hereafter. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The third: the first term He decreed is the time when He took the covenant from His creation while they were in the loins of Adam, and the second specified term with Him is life in this world. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: the term He decreed is the term of one who has died, and the specified term with Him is the term of one who will die afterward. This was said by Ibn Shajarah.

﴿you still doubt (tamtarun)﴾: Regarding this there are two meanings. The first: you doubt (tashukkun), and imtira' (dubiousness, doubting) is doubt. The second: you dispute (takhtalifun), derived from mira', which is disagreement.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth. He knows your secret and your open﴾: Regarding this there are three views. The first is that the meaning of the statement is: He is the Governor (al-Mudabbir) in the heavens and on the earth. ﴿He knows your secret and your open﴾, that is, what you conceal and what you proclaim.

The second: He is the God who is worshipped in the heavens and on the earth.

The third: there is a transposition (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the statement. Its meaning is: He is God, who knows your secret and your open in the heavens and on the earth, because in the heavens are the angels, and on the earth are humankind and the jinn. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿and He knows what you earn﴾: that is, what you do from now on, and nothing of what you have done is hidden from Him, nor what will happen, nor what you are in the present state of secrecy and openness.

﴿And if We had sent down to you a written scroll on paper﴾: because the polytheists of Quraysh denied the revelation of the Qur'an, God informed them that if He had sent it down to them from the sky, they would have denied it and disbelieved in it, due to the prevalence of corruption over them. Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

"Within them are trenches from the traces of their dwellers, as the pen moves back and forth over its paper (qirṭāsih)."

﴿So they touched it with their hands﴾: He said this to confirm its descent upon them.

There are three possible reasons for the touching of the hand rather than the seeing of the eye:

First: its descent would be with the angels, and they are not seen with the eyes; therefore it was expressed with touching rather than seeing.

Second: what is touched is closer than what is seen.

Third: magic can work upon things that are seen, but it cannot work upon things that are touched.

﴿Those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but evident magic (siḥrun mubīn)"﴾, a denial of the certainty, out of obstinacy. ﴿And they say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾: that is, an angel who would testify to his truthfulness. ﴿And if We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾: that is, if We had sent down an angel and they still did not believe, the matter would have been decided. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatada, because earlier nations, when they demanded signs from their prophets and God answered them by manifesting them, but they did not believe, He annihilated them with punishment.

The second: the meaning of "the matter would have been decided" is that the Hour would have been established. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-96) ﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾: that is, they would not be given respite nor delayed, meaning from the punishment of annihilation according to the first interpretation, and from the establishment of the Hour according to the second interpretation.

﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: meaning, if We had appointed with him an angel to indicate his truthfulness, We would have made it in the form of a man.

First: because the bodies of the angels are subtle and cannot be seen, so it was necessary that it be made a man, for the density of his body so that he could be seen.

Second: they would not be able to see the angels in their own forms, and if it were in the form of a man, they would not know whether it was an angel or not an angel.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 12–16:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day﴾ — of the bodies of living creatures, because among living creatures there are some that rest at night and some that rest by day.

If it is asked: Why did He say ﴿rests﴾ and not "moves"? It is answered, for two reasons. The first: rest encompasses more than movement does.

The second: because every moving thing must eventually have its motion come to rest, so every moving thing becomes at rest. al-Kalbi said: its meaning is "and to Him belongs whatever settles in the night and the day," and these two are the whole of time, for there is no time except night or day, and there is no division between them that falls outside either one of them.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector (wali)?﴾ — meaning, as a god who would take charge of me.

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ — that is, the Creator of the heavens and the earth and their Initiator (mubtadi'uha). Ibn 'Abbas said: "I did not know what Fatir meant until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said to his companion: 'I am the one who fatartuha'," that is, I initiated it. The root of fatr is splitting, and from it comes ﴿Do you see any rifts (futur)?﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], that is, cracks.

﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾ — its meaning is "He provides sustenance and is not provided for." Some read it ﴿wa huwa yut'imu wa la yut'am﴾, and its meaning according to this reading is: "He feeds His creation and does not eat."

﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit (aslama)﴾ — meaning, of his community. In this "submission" there are three aspects. The first: his surrender (istislam) to the command of Allah, and similar to this is the saying of the poet:

"The day lengthens for one who has no milk-camel, except for a gift, or abandonment with submission (bi-islam)"

that is, with surrender (bi-istislam).

The second: his entry into the peace (silm) of Allah and his exit from enmity toward Him.

The third: his entry into the religion of Ibrahim, as in His saying: ﴿The religion of your father Ibrahim; He named you "Muslims" before this﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. And the intended meaning would be the first of the Quraysh to submit, and it has been said: the first of the people of Makkah.

﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ — it is possible that this is an address from Allah to His Prophet, forbidding him from associating partners with Him, and it is possible that the intended meaning is his entire community, even though the address is directed to him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 17–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: its meaning is "If Allah inflicts harm upon you," because touching (al-mass) is not permissible upon Allah. The second: its meaning is "And if He causes harm to touch you."

Likewise His saying: ﴿And if He touches you with good﴾. And concerning harm (ad-durr) and good (al-khayr) there are two views. The first: harm is sickness and good is well-being. The second: harm is poverty and good is wealth.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: its meaning is "the Subduer of His servants," and "over" (fawq) is an extra connective particle. The second: that He, by His subjugation of His servants, is exalted above them, so His saying "over" (fawq) is used in its literal sense, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The hand of Allah is over their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10], because it is higher in power.

It may also be understood a third way: He is the Subduer above the subjugation of His servants, because His subjugation is above every subjugation.

Concerning this subjugation there are two views. The first: it is the bringing into existence of that which did not exist. The second: that there is none who can repel His decrees nor turn aside His choice.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony?﴾ up to the end of the verse. Concerning the occasion of its revelation (sabab nuzul) there are two views. The first: the polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Who will testify for you to prophethood?" So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse, commanding him to say to them: ﴿What thing is greatest in testimony?﴾ Then He answered that question, saying: ﴿Say: Allah is a witness between me and you﴾, meaning: to my truthfulness and the soundness of my prophethood, and this is the greatest of testimonies. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: Allah, may He be exalted, commanded him to bear witness against them to the conveying of the message to them, and He said this so that He might make him a witness against them.

﴿That I may warn you thereby, and whoever it reaches﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: "that I may warn you, O people of Makkah, and whoever the Qur'an has reached of people other than the people of Makkah." The second: "that I may warn you thereby, O Arabs, and whoever among the non-Arabs (al-'ajam) has been informed."

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Those whom We have given the Book﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: it refers to the Torah and the Gospel, as said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, as-Suddi, and Ibn Juraij. The second: it refers to the Qur'an.

﴿They recognize him as they recognize their sons﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: they recognize the Prophet ﷺ as they recognize their sons, because his description exists in their Book. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and those who claimed that the Book is the Torah and the Gospel.

The second: they recognize the Book which indicates his description, his truthfulness, and the soundness of his prophethood. This is the view of those who claimed that the Book is the Qur'an.

By His saying: ﴿as they recognize their sons﴾ He intended to affirm the certainty of the recognition.

Al-Kalbi and al-Farra' related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said to 'Abdullah ibn Salam when he embraced Islam: "What is this recognition by which you recognize Muhammad ﷺ as you recognize your sons?" He said: "By Allah, I recognize him when I see him better than I recognize my son, for I have no doubt that he is Muhammad, and I testify that he is true. And I do not know what the women have done concerning the son."

﴿Those who have lost themselves﴾. Concerning it there are two interpretations. The first: they lost, by disbelief, their dwellings and their spouses in Paradise, for there is no believer or disbeliever except that he has dwellings and spouses. If they embrace Islam, they are theirs; and if they disbelieve, they go to whoever among their people believed. This is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who inherit Paradise; therein they will abide forever﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 11]. This was said by al-Farra'.

The second: its meaning is that they defrauded themselves and destroyed them by disbelief and denial. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

He does not take a bribe in his judgment, nor does he care for the loss of the one who loses.

The first: its meaning is "If Allah inflicts harm upon you," because touching (al-mass) is not permissible upon Allah. The second: its meaning is "And if He causes harm to touch you."

Likewise His saying: ﴿And if He touches you with good﴾. And concerning harm (ad-durr) and good (al-khayr) there are two views. The first: harm is sickness and good is well-being. The second: harm is poverty and good is wealth.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: its meaning is "the Subduer of His servants," and "over" (fawq) is an extra connective particle. The second: that He, by His subjugation of His servants, is exalted above them, so His saying "over" (fawq) is used in its literal sense, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The hand of Allah is over their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10], because it is higher in power.

It may also be understood a third way: He is the Subduer above the subjugation of His servants, because His subjugation is above every subjugation.

Concerning this subjugation there are two views. The first: it is the bringing into existence of that which did not exist. The second: that there is none who can repel His decrees nor turn aside His choice.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony?﴾ up to the end of the verse. Concerning the occasion of its revelation (sabab nuzul) there are two views. The first: the polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Who will testify for you to prophethood?" So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse, commanding him to say to them: ﴿What thing is greatest in testimony?﴾ Then He answered that question, saying: ﴿Say: Allah is a witness between me and you﴾, meaning: to my truthfulness and the soundness of my prophethood, and this is the greatest of testimonies. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: Allah, may He be exalted, commanded him to bear witness against them to the conveying of the message to them, and He said this so that He might make him a witness against them.

﴿That I may warn you thereby, and whoever it reaches﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: "that I may warn you, O people of Makkah, and whoever the Qur'an has reached of people other than the people of Makkah." The second: "that I may warn you thereby, O Arabs, and whoever among the non-Arabs (al-'ajam) has been informed."

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Those whom We have given the Book﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: it refers to the Torah and the Gospel, as said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, as-Suddi, and Ibn Juraij. The second: it refers to the Qur'an.

﴿They recognize him as they recognize their sons﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: they recognize the Prophet ﷺ as they recognize their sons, because his description exists in their Book. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and those who claimed that the Book is the Torah and the Gospel.

The second: they recognize the Book which indicates his description, his truthfulness, and the soundness of his prophethood. This is the view of those who claimed that the Book is the Qur'an.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 22–26:**

﴿Then their trial will be only that they say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ and the rest of the verse.

On the word *fitnah* (trial, test) here there are three opinions. The first is that it means their excuse, and it is called *fitnah* because it arose from the *fitnah*. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second is that it means the consequence of their trial, which is their polytheism.

The third is that it means their affliction (*baliyyah*), which imposed the proof upon them and increased their blame. This is the view of Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam.

﴿Except that they said: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ They began with this from their polytheism. If it is asked: how could they lie in the Hereafter by denying polytheism, when lying is not possible for them in the Hereafter, for two reasons? The first is that it will not benefit them. The second is that they are turned away from ugly deeds and compelled (*mulja'un*) to abandon them, by the removal of *taklif* (moral obligation) from them. If they were not compelled to abandon the ugly deed and were not turned away from it, while their minds were complete, then they would have to be held accountable so that they might refrain from the ugly deed through it; and the absence of their being held accountable is evidence that they are compelled to abandon it.

It is said that there are two answers to this.

The first: their saying "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists" means, in the world, in their own estimation, because of their belief in it that they were upon the right course, even though its error became clear to them now. So this was not a lie on their part. This is the view of Qutrub.

The second: the Hereafter has stages. In one stage they do not know this and are not compelled to it, and in another stage they know it and are compelled to it. So they said that in the first stage. This is the view of some of the later theologians (*mutakallimun*).

(p-103) This is not correct, because it implies that they were held accountable in the first stage since there was no compulsion or necessity, and were not held accountable in the second stage.

The first answer may be objected to by His saying, after this verse: ﴿See how they lied against themselves.﴾ So He informed about them that they lied, while according to the first answer they were not liars.

This objection has been answered by a third answer, which is that they denied with their tongues, and when their limbs spoke, they acknowledged. In this answer there is a flaw, because they had denied the speech of the limbs.

﴿And what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.﴾ On this there are two interpretations. The first: by the evil of their lying and denial. The second: their idols, which they had fabricated against Allah by worshipping them, went astray from them. *Iftira'* (fabrication) is making a lie appear beautiful.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it.﴾ It is said that they used to listen at night to the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his prayer.

On this there are two interpretations. The first: they listened to his recitation in order to refute him. The second: to learn his place so that they might harm him. So Allah turned them away from hearing him, by casting sleep upon them, by placing over their hearts coverings so that they could not understand it.

*Akinnah* (coverings) are wrappings, singular *kinan*. It is said: "I covered the thing" (*kanantu al-shay'*) when I covered it, and "I concealed it within myself" (*akbantuhu*) when I hid it. In the recitation of 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud: "Over their eyes is a covering" (*ghita'*).

﴿And in their ears is deafness.﴾ *Waqr* is heaviness, and from it comes *waqar* (dignity), when a person is weighty in an assembly.

﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it.﴾ By "sign" is meant the mark of inimitability (*i'jaz*), because of what had become firmly established in their souls from their envy and hatred of him. This turned them away from hearing the Qur'an, because they intended by listening to it only harm and fabrication.

﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieved say: "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ Concerning what they used to dispute with the Prophet (ﷺ) there are two opinions. The first: they disputed with him using what Allah mentioned of their saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾ This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: it is their saying: "You eat what you have killed, and you do not eat what your Lord has killed." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The meaning of ﴿fables of the ancients﴾ is the narratives of the ancients that they used to write down (*yusattiruna*) in their books. It is said that the one who disputed with them using this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it.﴾ On this there are three opinions. The first: they forbid following Muhammad (ﷺ) and keep away from him, fleeing from him. This is the view of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi.

The second: they forbid the Qur'an to be acted upon by what is in it, and keep away from hearing it, lest knowledge of its truth should reach their hearts. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: they forbid harming Muhammad (ﷺ) and keep away from following him. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was revealed concerning Abu Talib. He used to forbid the polytheists from harming Muhammad (ﷺ), and he kept away from what he brought, so he did not believe in him, though the truthfulness of Muhammad was clear to him in himself."

Muqatil cited, as evidence for this, verses of Abu Talib's poetry that indicate it, with his saying:

*You called me and claimed that you were my sincere advisor, and indeed you spoke the truth, and you were trustworthy there.*
*And you presented a religion, which I know is among the best religions of mankind.*

*Were it not for reproach, or my fear of a reproach, you would have found me generous in this, clearly.*
*So go about your affair; there is no reproach upon you, and rejoice in that and let your eyes be cooled.*
*By Allah, they will never reach you with their gathering until I am laid beneath the dust, buried.*

Then this verse was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to him. Abu Talib said to him: "As for entering your religion, no." Ibn 'Abbas said: "[This was] for the precedence of the decree in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*)." This was also the view of 'Ata' and al-Qasim.

The second: they forbid the Qur'an to be acted upon by what is in it, and keep away from hearing it, lest knowledge of its truth should reach their hearts. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: they forbid harming Muhammad (ﷺ) and keep away from following him. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was revealed concerning Abu Talib. He used to forbid the polytheists from harming Muhammad (ﷺ), and he kept away from what he brought, so he did not believe in him, though the truthfulness of Muhammad was clear to him in himself."

Muqatil cited, as evidence for this, verses of Abu Talib's poetry that indicate it, with his saying:

*You called me and claimed that you were my sincere advisor, and indeed you spoke the truth, and you were trustworthy there.*
*And you presented a religion, which I know is among the best religions of mankind.*

*Were it not for reproach, or my fear of a reproach, you would have found me generous in this, clearly.*
*So go about your affair; there is no reproach upon you, and rejoice in that and let your eyes be cooled.*
*By Allah, they will never reach you with their gathering until I am laid beneath the dust, buried.*

Then this verse was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to him. Abu Talib said to him: "As for entering your religion, no." Ibn 'Abbas said: "[This was] for the precedence of the decree in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*)." This was also the view of 'Ata' and al-Qasim.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 22–26:**

﴿Then their trial will be only that they say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ and the rest of the verse.

On the word *fitnah* (trial, test) here there are three opinions. The first is that it means their excuse, and it is called *fitnah* because it arose from the *fitnah*. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second is that it means the consequence of their trial, which is their polytheism.

The third is that it means their affliction (*baliyyah*), which imposed the proof upon them and increased their blame. This is the view of Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam.

﴿Except that they said: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ They began with this from their polytheism. If it is asked: how could they lie in the Hereafter by denying polytheism, when lying is not possible for them in the Hereafter, for two reasons? The first is that it will not benefit them. The second is that they are turned away from ugly deeds and compelled (*mulja'un*) to abandon them, by the removal of *taklif* (moral obligation) from them. If they were not compelled to abandon the ugly deed and were not turned away from it, while their minds were complete, then they would have to be held accountable so that they might refrain from the ugly deed through it; and the absence of their being held accountable is evidence that they are compelled to abandon it.

It is said that there are two answers to this.

The first: their saying "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists" means, in the world, in their own estimation, because of their belief in it that they were upon the right course, even though its error became clear to them now. So this was not a lie on their part. This is the view of Qutrub.

The second: the Hereafter has stages. In one stage they do not know this and are not compelled to it, and in another stage they know it and are compelled to it. So they said that in the first stage. This is the view of some of the later theologians (*mutakallimun*).

(p-103) This is not correct, because it implies that they were held accountable in the first stage since there was no compulsion or necessity, and were not held accountable in the second stage.

The first answer may be objected to by His saying, after this verse: ﴿See how they lied against themselves.﴾ So He informed about them that they lied, while according to the first answer they were not liars.

This objection has been answered by a third answer, which is that they denied with their tongues, and when their limbs spoke, they acknowledged. In this answer there is a flaw, because they had denied the speech of the limbs.

﴿And what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.﴾ On this there are two interpretations. The first: by the evil of their lying and denial. The second: their idols, which they had fabricated against Allah by worshipping them, went astray from them. *Iftira'* (fabrication) is making a lie appear beautiful.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, but We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it.﴾ It is said that they used to listen at night to the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his prayer.

On this there are two interpretations. The first: they listened to his recitation in order to refute him. The second: to learn his place so that they might harm him. So Allah turned them away from hearing him, by casting sleep upon them, by placing over their hearts coverings so that they could not understand it.

*Akinnah* (coverings) are wrappings, singular *kinan*. It is said: "I covered the thing" (*kanantu al-shay'*) when I covered it, and "I concealed it within myself" (*akbantuhu*) when I hid it. In the recitation of 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud: "Over their eyes is a covering" (*ghita'*).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 27–30:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: they witnessed it (ʿayānūhā), and whoever witnesses a thing has "stood" before it. The second: it was beneath them while they were above it, so they became those who stood over it. The third: they recognized it by entering into it, and whoever recognizes a thing has "stood" before it.

Al-Kalbi mentioned a fourth interpretation: its meaning is "And if you could see when they are held back (ḥubisū) before the Fire."

﴿So they will say, "Oh, would that we could be returned and not deny the signs of our Lord and be among the believers."﴾ They wished to be returned to the world, which is the abode of responsibility (dār al-taklīf), so that they might believe and affirm. A wish (al-tamannī) admits neither truth nor falsehood, because it is not a report (khabar).

(p-106) Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿But there has appeared to them what they had been concealing before﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings. The first: there appeared to them the consequence (wabāl) of what they had been concealing. The second: there appeared to them what some of them had been hiding from others, as said by al-Hasan. The third: there appeared to the followers what the leaders had been hiding.

﴿And if they were returned, they would return to that which they were forbidden﴾, meaning: even if they were returned to what they wished for of the world, they would return to what they had been forbidden of disbelief.

﴿And indeed, they are liars﴾. Regarding this there are two sayings. One: it is a new, independent statement, through which God informs of their lying, and it does not refer back to their earlier wish, since wishing admits neither truth nor falsehood. The second: ﴿And indeed, they are liars﴾ means in their reporting about themselves, that they would believe if they were returned.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 31–32:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but play and amusement﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: "And the affair of this world and the work done for it is nothing but play and amusement." As for performing righteous deeds in it, that is from the work of the Hereafter, so it is removed from being play and amusement.

The second: "And the people of the life of this world are nothing but people of play and amusement, due to their being occupied with it over what is better than it." This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri).

The third: "That they are like the people of play and amusement, because their pleasures are cut off and their duration is short, while the people of the Hereafter are the opposite of them, due to the lastingness of their duration and the continuity of their pleasure." This is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the Abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of Allah﴾, because what was cut off for them elsewhere has lasted for them there.

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ [that this is better for you].

Some of the al-Khatiriyya (an early group of Mu'tazila-linked scholars) mentioned a fourth opinion: that it is play for the one who gathers it, and amusement for the one who inherits it.

The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿We certainly know that what they say grieves you﴾, meaning, their denial of you and their disbelief in Me.

﴿So it is not you they deny﴾. On this there are four interpretations. The first: they do not deny you with any proof; it is only denial of obstinacy and stubbornness, so do not be grieved, for it does not harm you. This was said by Abu Salih, Qatada and al-Suddi.

The second: they do not deny your speech, because they know you are truthful, but they deny what you have brought. This was said by Najiyah ibn Ka'b.

The third: they do not deny you in private, because they know you are truthful, but they deny you openly, out of their enmity towards you. This was said by al-Kalbi.

(p-108) The fourth: its meaning is that their denial of your message is not a denial of you, because you are a messenger who conveys, and it is only a denial of My signs, which indicate your truthfulness and make acceptance of your speech obligatory. He explained this with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of God﴾, that is, they lie.

Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read ﴿they do not deny you﴾ (lā yukadhdhibūnaka). This is a qira'ah (a recognised variant reading of the Qur'an) reported from the Prophet (ﷺ). Its interpretation is: they do not find you to be a liar.

The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And none can alter the words of God﴾. It admits four interpretations. The first: its meaning is that none can nullify His proof or repel His demonstration.

The second: its meaning is that none can reject His command in what He has decreed of the victory of His friends and what He has made obligatory of the destruction of His enemies.

The third: its meaning is that there is no denial of His report in what He has related of the victory of those who were victorious and the destruction of those who were destroyed.

The fourth: its meaning is that what the liars have fabricated against Him is not confused with what the prophets have conveyed from Him.

﴿And there has already come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾, concerning what they endured of harm and what they were recompensed with of victory.

The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And if their turning away has been difficult for you﴾. On this there are two views. The first: their turning away from listening to the Qur'an. The second: their turning away from your listening (to them).

﴿So if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth﴾: that is, a burrow (sirb), which is the passage within it, derived from the concealed exit (nāfiqā') of the jerboa (yarbū').

﴿Or a ladder into the sky﴾. On this there are three sayings: (p-109) The first: a means of ascent, said by al-Suddi. The second: steps, said by Qatada. The third: a cause (sabab), said by al-Kalbi. The saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr includes this meaning:

"Nor is there for the two of you a refuge on the earth, so seek with it a tunnel, or a ladder into the heavens."

﴿Then you bring them a sign﴾, that is, a sign better than your sign, and you will not be able to do that; they will not believe you. So do not be grieved by their denial and disbelief. Al-Farra' said: in the speech there is an implied omission, and its estimate is: "then bring them a sign," so do it.

﴿And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾, that is, by compulsion and constraint.

Ibn Abbas said: wherever God says ﴿And if God had willed﴾, He did not will it.

﴿So never be among the ignorant﴾, that is, do not lament in situations requiring patience, lest through grief and regret you come to resemble the states of the ignorant.

The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Only those who listen respond﴾. Response (istijābah) is acceptance, and the difference between it and answer (jawāb) is that an answer may be acceptance or not acceptance.

His saying ﴿those who listen﴾ admits two interpretations. The first: it means those who understand, said by al-Kalbi. The second: those who listen seeking the truth, because response may come only from those who listen seeking the truth. As for one who does not listen, or who listens but not with the intention of seeking the truth, there is no response from him.

The second: they do not deny your speech, because they know you are truthful, but they deny what you have brought. This was said by Najiyah ibn Ka'b.

The third: they do not deny you in private, because they know you are truthful, but they deny you openly, out of their enmity towards you. This was said by al-Kalbi.

(p-108) The fourth: its meaning is that their denial of your message is not a denial of you, because you are a messenger who conveys, and it is only a denial of My signs, which indicate your truthfulness and make acceptance of your speech obligatory. He explained this with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of God﴾, that is, they lie.

Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read ﴿they do not deny you﴾ (lā yukadhdhibūnaka). This is a qira'ah (a recognised variant reading of the Qur'an) reported from the Prophet (ﷺ). Its interpretation is: they do not find you to be a liar.

The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And none can alter the words of God﴾. It admits four interpretations. The first: its meaning is that none can nullify His proof or repel His demonstration.

The second: its meaning is that none can reject His command in what He has decreed of the victory of His friends and what He has made obligatory of the destruction of His enemies.

The third: its meaning is that there is no denial of His report in what He has related of the victory of those who were victorious and the destruction of those who were destroyed.

The fourth: its meaning is that what the liars have fabricated against Him is not confused with what the prophets have conveyed from Him.

﴿And there has already come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾, concerning what they endured of harm and what they were recompensed with of victory.

The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And if their turning away has been difficult for you﴾. On this there are two views. The first: their turning away from listening to the Qur'an. The second: their turning away from your listening (to them).

﴿So if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth﴾: that is, a burrow (sirb), which is the passage within it, derived from the concealed exit (nāfiqā') of the jerboa (yarbū').

﴿Or a ladder into the sky﴾. On this there are three sayings: (p-109) The first: a means of ascent, said by al-Suddi. The second: steps, said by Qatada. The third: a cause (sabab), said by al-Kalbi. The saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr includes this meaning:

"Nor is there for the two of you a refuge on the earth, so seek with it a tunnel, or a ladder into the heavens."

﴿Then you bring them a sign﴾, that is, a sign better than your sign, and you will not be able to do that; they will not believe you. So do not be grieved by their denial and disbelief. Al-Farra' said: in the speech there is an implied omission, and its estimate is: "then bring them a sign," so do it.

﴿And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾, that is, by compulsion and constraint.

Ibn Abbas said: wherever God says ﴿And if God had willed﴾, He did not will it.

﴿So never be among the ignorant﴾, that is, do not lament in situations requiring patience, lest through grief and regret you come to resemble the states of the ignorant.

The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Only those who listen respond﴾. Response (istijābah) is acceptance, and the difference between it and answer (jawāb) is that an answer may be acceptance or not acceptance.

His saying ﴿those who listen﴾ admits two interpretations. The first: it means those who understand, said by al-Kalbi. The second: those who listen seeking the truth, because response may come only from those who listen seeking the truth. As for one who does not listen, or who listens but not with the intention of seeking the truth, there is no response from him.

﴿As for the dead, God will raise them﴾. On this there are two views. The first: that by "the dead" here are meant the disbelievers, said by al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid.

The meaning of the speech then is: only the believers who listen respond, while the disbelievers do not listen except at the moment of directly witnessing the truth, under compulsion, when it no longer benefits them, until God raises them as disbelievers, then they are gathered as disbelievers.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 37–39:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say: "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ That is, a sign that would serve as proof of his truthfulness and the soundness of his prophethood.

﴿Say: "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign"﴾ That is, a sign by which they would be answered in what they asked for.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ This admits of two meanings.

The first: they do not know the benefit in sending down the sign.

The second: they do not know that, if signs are multiplied while they do not believe in them, this increases their punishment, because of the abundance of their denial.

If it is said: this verse does not indicate that Allah did not send down to them a sign that would lead them to belief, so that belief would not be obligatory for them. It is said: this is an error, because the signs that Allah manifested, which indicate the truthfulness of His Messenger and the soundness of his prophethood, are too evident to be concealed and too numerous to be denied. The Qur'an, together with the inability of those whom Allah challenged to produce its like, and what it contains of reports of the unseen and the truthfulness of its account of what has been and what will be, is the most eloquent of signs and the most manifest of miracles.

They only proposed a sign which they requested in order to cause difficulty, so they were not answered, although Allah is able to send it down. For if He had answered them with it, they would have proposed other signs without end, until the Messenger was cut off, by the manifestation of signs, from conveying the message.

The manifestation of signs is obligatory only in two situations. The first: when he is sent as a messenger, so that his summons is accompanied by a proof of his truthfulness. The second: when someone asks for it whom Allah knows would believe if He manifested it to him. It is not obligatory for him to manifest signs outside these two situations.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there is no creature moving on the earth﴾ "Creature" (dābbah) means every living animal that crawls upon the earth.

﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ That is, in the air. He combined what is upon the earth and within it with what rises above it.

﴿except that they are communities like you﴾ Regarding "communities" (umam) there are two interpretations. The first: that they are groups. The second: that they are kinds, as said by al-Farra'.

By His saying ﴿like you﴾ He does not intend equality in taklif (legal and moral obligation), as some people did, whose apparent meaning was confused for them, and who, despite the confusion of the apparent meaning, relied on the narration of Abu Dharr, who said: "Two sheep butted each other in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know why they butted each other?' I said: 'No.' He said: '(But Allah knows, and He will judge between them).'" Abu Dharr said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ left us, and no bird flaps its wings in the sky without his having given us knowledge of it." Because, if reason is the cause of taklif, then its absence entails the removal of taklif.

By His saying ﴿like you﴾ there are two meanings. The first: that they are kinds, distinguished in forms and names. The second: that they are created beings who are not wronged, and provided for beings who are not deprived.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: We have not left any creature without appointing for it a term (ajal). Here "the Book" is the appointment of the term, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿For every term there is a Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38]. This was said by Ibn Bahr, who recited the verse of Nabigha Bani Ja'dah:

"They reached the kings, and they attained the Book, and the term came to its end."

The second interpretation, which is the saying of the majority, is that the Book is the noble Qur'an which He sent down, in which He omitted nothing of the matters of the religion, whether stated in detail, needing no explanation, or stated in summary, for which He made a way to its explanation.

It admits of a third interpretation: We have not neglected in it by letting a flaw enter it, or by the presence of a deficiency in it. The Book of Allah is free of deficiency and flaw.

﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: that by gathering (hashr) is meant death, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that gathering is the assembling for the resurrection of the Hour.

If it is said: if they are not under taklif, then why are they resurrected on the Day of Resurrection? It is said: taklif is not the cause of resurrection, because children and the insane are resurrected even though in this world they were not under taklif. Rather, He resurrects them so that He may compensate whatever deserved compensation from them for pain or injustice, then He makes of them whatever He wills dust, and whatever He wills of the beasts of Paradise the believers enjoy by riding them and beholding them.

**The Qur'an:** ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾. The meaning is that they abandoned what God had reminded them of from His signs, which indicate His oneness and the truthfulness of His Messenger.

﴿We opened for them the gates of everything﴾, meaning the blessings of this world and abundance of provision.

Regarding God's bestowal of favours upon them despite their disbelief, there are two possibilities. The first is that His favour upon them should call them to faith. The second is that it should be a gradual lure (istidraj, a gradual leading into ruin) and a trial. Ibn Lahi'a related with his chain of narration from Uqba ibn Amir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If you see God giving His servants what they wish while they persist in disobeying Him, then that is istidraj from Him," and then he recited: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ (p-114) ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given﴾, meaning the blessings, and they did not believe.

﴿We seized them suddenly﴾. This may bear two interpretations.

The first is that it is the hastening of a destroying punishment, as a recompense for two things: the first being their disbelief in Him, and the second their disbelief in His blessings.

The second interpretation is the swift coming of death while they are heedless of it through blessings, cutting off their pleasure and inflicting the torment of regret.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿then they were suddenly despairing﴾. Regarding this there are five interpretations.

The first: that iblas means despair (iyas). Adi ibn Zayd said:

*A king who, when the needy come to his door, they envy him, and the one among them who is despairing (al-mustabliss) attains more success.*

meaning the one who is in despair.

The second: that it is grief and remorse.

The third: humility.

The fourth: abandonment (khidhlan).

The fifth: silence and the cutting off of argument. From this is the saying of al-Ajjaj:

*O friend, do you recognize a faded, worn-out trace?
He said: Yes, I recognize it, and it has grown mute.*

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 46–54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of Allah﴾. It has two interpretations. The first: the provision, meaning I am not able to make a poor man rich or a rich man poor. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: the keys to the treasuries of punishment, because he warned them of it, so they said: "When will this happen?" This was said by Muqatil.

﴿Nor do I know the unseen﴾. It has two interpretations. The first: knowledge of the unseen regarding when the punishment will descend upon them. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: knowledge of everything hidden, whether past or future, except that the future is not known except by Allah or by those among His prophets whom Allah informs of His knowledge. As for the past, created beings may know it in one of two ways: either by direct witnessing or by report. If the report is about the future, it is one of the miraculous signs of Allah. If it is about the past, and someone other than the informant and the one informed knows of it, it is not a miracle. But if no one knows of it except the informant alone, it is a miracle. Thus the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) denied of himself knowledge of the unseen, because none knows it except Allah, the exalted. Whatever he reported of the unseen was from Allah and His revelation.

﴿Nor do I say to you that I am an angel﴾. It has two interpretations. The first: he means that he is not able to do what the servants are unable to do, even if the angels are able to do it.

The second: he means by this that he is among the human beings and is not an angel, to negate from himself the exaggeration of the Christians regarding the Messiah and their saying that he is the son of Allah.

Then, regarding his denial that he is an angel, there are two interpretations. The first: by this he clarified the superiority of the angels over the prophets, because he repelled from himself a rank that was not his.

The second: he meant, "I am not an angel in the heavens, so as to know the unseen of the heavens that the angels witness and that is hidden from human beings." Although the prophets are more excellent than the angels, they are unaware of what the angels witness.

﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: I only inform you of what Allah has informed me. 

(p-117) The second: I only do what Allah has commanded me to do.

﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ This may have two meanings. The first: the ignorant and the knowing. 

The second: the disbelievers and the believers.

﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ This may have two meanings. The first: concerning the parable Allah has struck of the blind and the seeing. 

The second: concerning what He has made clear of His signs that indicate His oneness and the truthfulness of His Messenger.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾. It is narrated that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was that "the chiefs of Quraysh came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and with him was a group of the weak among the Muslims, such as Bilal, Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, and Ibn Mas'ud. They said: 'O Muhammad, drive away from us your clients and allies, for they are only our slaves and freedmen. Perhaps if you drive them away we will follow you.' Umar said: 'If you did that, we would know what they want and where they will end up.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to do so, until this verse was revealed."

And there was revealed concerning the chiefs of Quraysh: ﴿And thus We have tested some of them by means of others﴾, the verse. Then Umar came and apologized for his statement, so Allah revealed concerning him: ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you﴾, the verse.

Regarding His saying, ﴿those who call upon their Lord﴾, there are four interpretations. The first: they are the five daily prayers. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: that it is the remembrance of Allah. This was said by Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

The third: the glorification of the Qur'an. This was said by Abu Ja'far.

(p-118) The fourth: that it is the worship of Allah. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Regarding the meaning of His saying, ﴿seeking His face﴾, there are two views. The first: they seek by their supplication. For the Arabs mention the face of a thing to mean desiring it, like their saying: "This is the face of the right course," as an exaltation and magnification of the matter.

The second: its meaning is that they seek His obedience, by their intention toward the direction to which He has turned them.

﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning in anything﴾. There are three statements regarding this. The first: it means you are not accountable for the reckoning of their deeds, in any respect, of reward or punishment.

﴿Nor are they accountable for your reckoning in anything﴾. It means: nor is the reckoning of your deeds upon them in anything, because each person is held accountable only for the reckoning of his own deeds, and no one else's. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: its meaning is: you are not accountable for their provision and their poverty in anything.

The third: you are not responsible for their sustenance, nor are they responsible for yours. Al-hisab here means sufficiency, like His saying: ﴿a gift, sufficient (hisaban)﴾ [al-Naba' 78:36], meaning complete and adequate. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We have tested some of them by means of others﴾, meaning through their differences in provisions, characters, and circumstances.

Regarding Allah's testing of them there are two views. The first: that it is their trial and examination, so that He may test by it the gratitude of the rich and the patience of the poor. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: the imposition of what is hard upon the self while it is able to bear it.

﴿So that they may say: Is it these whom Allah has favored among us?﴾ This is the statement of the chiefs of Quraysh (p-119) about the weak among the believers. Regarding what Allah, may He be exalted, favored them with, there are two views. The first: the kindness Allah bestowed upon them in their faith.

The second: what He mentioned of their gratitude for His obedience.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you﴾. By this He means the weak among the Muslims, and what had occurred concerning Umar.

﴿Then say: Peace be upon you﴾. There are two views regarding this. The first: that he was commanded by Allah, may He be exalted, to greet them with peace. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that he was commanded to greet them with peace from himself, as an honor to them. This was said by some of the later scholars.

Regarding "peace" (al-salam) there are two views. The first: that it gathers the meaning of safety (al-salamah).

The second: that al-Salam is Allah Himself, and its meaning is "the Possessor of peace."

﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾. There are two views regarding this. The first: its meaning is that Allah obligated upon Himself.

The second: He wrote it on Himself in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

As for ﴿mercy﴾, the intended meaning here may be of two kinds. The first: aid. 

The second: pardon.

﴿That whoever of you does evil out of ignorance﴾. Regarding "ignorance" there are two interpretations. (p-120) The first: it is sin. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak.

The second: it is doing something whose consequence one dislikes without knowing it. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

A third possibility is also conceivable: that ignorance here means committing a doubtful matter through a faulty interpretation.

﴿Then repents after it and makes amends﴾. Meaning: he repents of his past deed and sets right his conduct in the future.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 46–54:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Say: Indeed, I am upon clear evidence from my Lord⦘. Regarding "clear evidence" (bayyinah) here there are two opinions. The first: the truth that has become manifest to him.

The second: the miraculous (mu'jiz) Qur'an.

﴿And you have denied it⦘. Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: you have denied the clear evidence.

The second: you have denied your Lord.

(p-121) ﴿What you are hastening for is not with me⦘. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: what they are hastening for of the punishment with which they were threatened before its time, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment⦘. This is said by al-Hasan.

The second: what they sought hastily of the demanding of signs, because it is the seeking of a thing outside its time. This is said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah⦘. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: the judgment concerning reward and punishment.

The second: the judgment in distinguishing the truth from falsehood.

﴿He relates the truth⦘. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Asim read ﴿yaqussu⦘ with an unpointed sad, from qasas, which is reporting it. The rest read "yaqdi" with a pointed dad, from qada', which is the making and completion of the truth.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him⦘. Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: the treasuries of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and of provisions and decrees, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Abbas.

The second: arriving at knowledge of the unseen.

﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it⦘, meaning before it dries and falls.

﴿Nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth⦘ may bear two aspects: (p-122) The first: what is in its belly of seed.

The second: what it brings forth of crops.

﴿Nor anything fresh or dry⦘ may bear two aspects: The first: that the fresh refers to vegetation and the dry to solid substances.

The second: that the fresh is the living and the dry is the dead.

﴿Except that it is in a clear Record⦘, meaning in the Preserved Tablet.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him⦘. Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: the treasuries of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and of provisions and decrees, and this is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Abbas.

The second: arriving at knowledge of the unseen.

﴿And He knows what is in the land and the sea⦘. Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: that what is in the land is what is upon the earth, and what is in the sea is what is upon the water, and this is the apparent meaning; the majority held this view.

The second: that the land means the barren wilderness and the sea means the settlements, because water exists in them, and therefore they were named "sea." This is said by Mujahid.

﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it⦘, meaning before it dries and falls.

﴿Nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth⦘ may bear two aspects: (p-122) The first: what is in its belly of seed.

The second: what it brings forth of crops.

﴿Nor anything fresh or dry⦘ may bear two aspects: The first: that the fresh refers to vegetation and the dry to solid substances.

The second: that the fresh is the living and the dry is the dead.

**Al-Mawardi's commentary (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah 6, verses 60–62:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, words: ﴿It is He who takes your souls by night﴾. He means by it sleep, because in it He seizes the souls from activity, just as He seizes them by death. From this is the poet's saying:

Indeed the sons of al-Ardad are not of anyone, and Quraysh does not take them into account in the count.

That is, Quraysh does not seize them (lā tuqabbiduhum).

﴿And He knows what you have earned (jaraḥtum) by day﴾: that is, what you have acquired, because it is gained through the action of the limb (jāriḥah). From this comes "jawāriḥ al-ṭayr" (the birds of prey), because they are "kawāsib" (earners) by their talons. The "jarḥ" of testimony is the attacking of it, because it is the acquisition of sin. This was said by al-A'shā:

He is the one who repels from one in distress the hands of the people, when the offender commits a crime.

﴿Then He raises you up in it﴾: that is, in the day, through wakefulness, and the soul is returned after its seizure in sleep.

﴿That a term appointed may be fulfilled﴾: that is, the completion of the lifespan and the ending of the term by death.

﴿Then to Him is your return﴾: that is, by the resurrection and the rising up on the Day of Judgment.

﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ in the world, of good and evil.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, words: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. In it there are two views. The first: He is higher in subjugation, and therefore He said ﴿over His servants﴾. The second: when the one who is more capable merits the attribute of intensification, he is described with this kind of expression, and it is said, "He is above him in power," meaning "more capable," and "above him in knowledge," meaning "more knowing."

﴿And He sends over you guardians (ḥafaẓah)﴾. In it there are two views. The first: they are their limbs which testify against them concerning what they used to do. The second: the angels.

The word ﴿ḥafaẓah﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: the preservation of souls from calamities. The second: the preservation of deeds, good and evil, so that knowledge of their being recorded may be a stronger deterrent from evil and a stronger incentive toward good.

﴿Until, when death comes to one of you﴾: that is, the causes of death, through the ending of the term.

If it is said: the one charged with seizing the soul is the Angel of Death, and this is explained by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11]. Then how does He say ﴿Our messengers take him (tawaffathu rusulunā)﴾, when "rusul" is plural?

It is said: because Allah aided the Angel of Death with helpers from Him, who carry out that by His command. So the taking becomes the act of his helpers, and it is attributed to him because of his command, just as the act of a ruler's helpers, such as killing or flogging, is attributed to the ruler when it is done by his command.

﴿And they do not neglect (yufarriṭūn)﴾: in it there are two views. The first: they do not delay. The second: they do not waste, as said by Ibn 'Abbās.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, words: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master (mawlāhum al-ḥaqq)﴾. Concerning who performs the returning there are two views. The first: they are the angels who took them. The second: it is Allah, by the resurrection and the rising up.

Concerning their return to Allah there are two views. The first: its meaning is their return to the sole management of Allah, because Allah managed them at their creation and origination, granted them the ability to act, so they were in charge of their own affairs; then He withheld them from that by death, so they returned to the management of Allah as in the first state, and by that they were returned to Him. The second: they were returned to the place where none but Allah holds judgment over them, so the return to that place was called a return to Him.

If it is asked: how does He say ﴿their true Master (mawlāhumu al-ḥaqq)﴾ when He has said ﴿That is because Allah is the Master (mawlā) of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no master﴾ [Muhammad: 11]? It is answered: there are two responses concerning this. The first: He said this because they entered into the general body of others among the believers who are returned, so the wording encompassed them. The second: "mawlā" is sometimes used to mean a helper and sometimes to mean a lord, and Allah is not a helper of the disbelievers, though He is the Lord of both the disbelievers and the believers.

The word ﴿al-ḥaqq﴾ here may bear three meanings. The first: that al-Ḥaqq is one of His names, Exalted is He. The second: because He is the one deserving that they return to Him. The third: because of His judgment regarding them, that they be returned.

﴿Is not judgment His? (alā lahu al-ḥukm)﴾: that is, the deciding between His servants.

If it is said: has judgment not been given to others? There are two responses concerning this. The first: judgment belongs to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection. The second: others judge by His command, so judgment belongs to Him.

The word ﴿alā lahu al-ḥukm﴾ may bear a second meaning: that He has the right to judge for Himself, and by this judgment He becomes the exclusive one.

﴿And He is the swiftest of reckoners (asraʿu al-ḥāsibīn)﴾. It may bear two meanings. The first: the swiftness of judgment among the servants, to hasten the decision; and He expressed judgment by reckoning, from the verification of one who fully receives both the little and the much. The second, and it is the apparent one, is that He intended the swiftness of the reckoning of the servants for their deeds.

His intended meaning by the swiftness of His reckoning may bear two meanings. The first: displaying His power by hastening what others cannot do. The second: that by it He shows the hastening of what is due to the one deserving reward, and the hastening of what is due to the one deserving punishment, combining His justice (inṣāf) and His vindication (intiṣāf).

(p-126) His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Say: "He is able to send upon you a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet"﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

First: the punishment from above them is stoning, and the punishment from beneath their feet is being swallowed up by the earth. This was said by Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Abu Malik.

Second: the punishment from above them is evil rulers (a'immat al-su'), and the punishment from beneath their feet is evil subordinates ('abid al-su'). This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Third: the punishment from above them is the flood, and the punishment from beneath their feet is the wind. This was related by Ali ibn Isa.

It is also possible that the punishment from above them refers to the calamities of the sky that are not from the deeds of people, because they are above them, and the punishment from beneath their feet refers to what comes from the deeds of people, because the earth is beneath the feet of all of them.

﴿Or confound you with factions﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations: First: they are the fabricated desires (al-ahwa' al-mukhtalaqah), said by Ibn Abbas.

Second: they are strife and discord, said by Mujahid.

It is also possible, thirdly, that it means: He will set over you your followers, who were your partisans, so they will become your enemies after they had been your allies. This is among the most severe forms of retribution, that the lowly should dominate the noble.

It has been narrated that Musa ibn Imran (peace be upon him) prayed to his Lord against a people, and God revealed to him: "Is this not the painful, swift punishment?"

This is the view of the exegetes of the apparent meaning (ahl al-zahir). But some of the deep thinkers (al-mutaʿammiqin) in the subtleties of the meanings (p-127) interpreted ﴿a punishment from above you﴾ as the sins of hearing, sight and tongue, and ﴿or from beneath your feet﴾ as walking toward sins until one commits them, and what lies between them is taken according to the nearer of the two. ﴿Or confound you with factions﴾ means: He removes affection from among you.

﴿And make some of you taste the violence of others﴾: the takfir of the people of the (false) passions one another. But the view of the majority: ﴿And make some of you taste the violence of others﴾ means with wars and killing, until some of them destroy others, because He did not make victory for some of them so that they would remain.

﴿See how We vary the signs﴾ may bear two meanings: First: We detail the signs of punishment and the kinds of retribution.

Second: We direct each kind of sign to a people, and it is not beyond Us to gather them upon one people.

﴿That perhaps they may understand﴾, i.e., that they may take admonition and so refrain.

The interpreters differed concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, on two views: First: that it concerns the people of prayer (ahl al-salah), said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada. "And its revelation distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), [so] he stood and prayed the forenoon prayer (salat al-duha) and prolonged it. It was said to him: 'You have never prolonged a prayer like today.' He said: '(It is a prayer of hope and fear. I asked my Lord to protect me from four things, and He protected me from two and did not protect me from two. I asked Him that He not destroy my community with a punishment from above them as He did to the people of Noah and the people of Lot, and He protected me. I asked Him that He not destroy my community with a punishment from beneath their feet as He did to Qarun, and He protected me. I asked Him that He not divide them into factions, and He did not protect me. I asked Him that He not make some of them taste the violence of others, and He did not protect me.)' And there was revealed to him the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1-2]."

(p-128) The second view: that it was revealed concerning the polytheists (mushrikun), said by some of the later scholars.

It is also possible, thirdly, that it means: He will set over you your followers, who were your partisans, so they will become your enemies after they had been your allies. This is among the most severe forms of retribution, that the lowly should dominate the noble.

It has been narrated that Musa ibn Imran (peace be upon him) prayed to his Lord against a people, and God revealed to him: "Is this not the painful, swift punishment?"

This is the view of the exegetes of the apparent meaning (ahl al-zahir). But some of the deep thinkers (al-mutaʿammiqin) in the subtleties of the meanings (p-127) interpreted ﴿a punishment from above you﴾ as the sins of hearing, sight and tongue, and ﴿or from beneath your feet﴾ as walking toward sins until one commits them, and what lies between them is taken according to the nearer of the two. ﴿Or confound you with factions﴾ means: He removes affection from among you.

﴿And make some of you taste the violence of others﴾: the takfir of the people of the (false) passions one another. But the view of the majority: ﴿And make some of you taste the violence of others﴾ means with wars and killing, until some of them destroy others, because He did not make victory for some of them so that they would remain.

﴿See how We vary the signs﴾ may bear two meanings: First: We detail the signs of punishment and the kinds of retribution.

Second: We direct each kind of sign to a people, and it is not beyond Us to gather them upon one people.

﴿That perhaps they may understand﴾, i.e., that they may take admonition and so refrain.

The interpreters differed concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, on two views: First: that it concerns the people of prayer (ahl al-salah), said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada. "And its revelation distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), [so] he stood and prayed the forenoon prayer (salat al-duha) and prolonged it. It was said to him: 'You have never prolonged a prayer like today.' He said: '(It is a prayer of hope and fear. I asked my Lord to protect me from four things, and He protected me from two and did not protect me from two. I asked Him that He not destroy my community with a punishment from above them as He did to the people of Noah and the people of Lot, and He protected me. I asked Him that He not destroy my community with a punishment from beneath their feet as He did to Qarun, and He protected me. I asked Him that He not divide them into factions, and He did not protect me. I asked Him that He not make some of them taste the violence of others, and He did not protect me.)' And there was revealed to him the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1-2]."

(p-128) The second view: that it was revealed concerning the polytheists (mushrikun), said by some of the later scholars.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 66–69:**

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Your people denied it, though it is the truth.﴾ Regarding what they denied, there are two opinions. The first: it is the Qur'an, as said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The second: it is the clarification of the verses (tasrif al-ayat), as said by some of the later scholars.

﴿And it is the truth﴾ means what they denied. The difference between al-Haqq (the truth) and al-Sawab (the correct, the right) is that al-Haqq may be attained without seeking, whereas al-Sawab is not attained except through seeking.

﴿Say: I am not a guardian over you﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: its meaning is, I am not a watcher over your deeds to requite you for them; I am only a warner. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: I am not a watcher over you who would prevent you from disbelieving, as a guardian (wakil) over a thing prevents harm from reaching it. This was said by some of the later scholars.

The third: its meaning is, I do not take you to faith by compulsion and coercion, as a wakil takes hold of a thing. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

(p-129) ﴿For every news there is a fixed time, and you will come to know﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: its meaning is that for every report which Allah, exalted is He, has informed of, whether a promise or a threat, there is a fixed occurrence in the future, the past, or the present, in this world and in the Hereafter. This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: it is a threat from Allah to the disbelievers in the Hereafter, because they do not acknowledge the Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: it is a threat to them concerning what will befall them in this world. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Nor is there anything upon those who fear Allah for their reckoning, of anything﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: nothing is upon those who fear Allah in His commands and prohibitions for the reckoning of the disbelievers concerning what they did of mockery and denial, as sins for which they are taken to account; rather, it is incumbent upon them to remind them of Allah and His signs, perhaps they will fear what they are upon of mockery and denial. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: nothing is upon those who fear Allah regarding the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection, what is upon the disbelievers in the reckoning of severity and harshness, because the reckoning of the God-fearing is a reminder and lightening, while the reckoning of the disbelievers is severity and harshness, perhaps they will fear when they know that.

The third: nothing is upon those who fear Allah for what they did of rejection and turning away from reckoning; rather, turn to reminding them with speech before action, perhaps they will fear when they know.

This interpretation may bear two meanings: the first: they fear mockery and denial. The second: they fear the warning and threat.
