Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 70:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾. There are two opinions concerning them. The first: they are the disbelievers who mock the signs of God when they hear them. This was said by Ali ibn Isa.

The second: there is no people who have a festival in which they amuse themselves except the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), for their festivals are prayer, glorification of God (takbir), piety and goodness. This was said by al-Farra'.

﴿And the life of this world has deceived them﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: its meaning is that the life of this world deceived them by (the expectation of) safety in it and attaining what they sought from it.

The second: its meaning is that the world deceived them with life and with safety from it. So the deception is by life in the first interpretation, and by the world in the second.

﴿And remind with it, lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned﴾. It has been said its meaning is: lest it be delivered to destruction, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [An-Nisa: 176], meaning: lest you go astray.

In His saying ﴿lest it be delivered to destruction﴾ there are six interpretations. The first: lest it be delivered (to ruin), said by al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: lest it be detained, said by Qatadah.

The third: lest it be disgraced, said by Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: lest it be seized for what it has earned, said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: lest it be recompensed, said by al-Kalbi.

The sixth: lest it be held in pledge, said by al-Farra', from the saying of them: a lion is "basil" (brave), because its prey is held in pledge with it and does not escape from it. From this is the saying of Awf ibn al-Ahwas al-Kilabi: (p-131)

Wa-ibsali buniya bi-ghayri jurmin ba'anāhu wa-la bi-damin muraqin

His saying "ba'anahu" means "janaynahu" (I committed it). The root of al-ibsal is prohibition, from their saying: "sharabun basl," meaning forbidden drink. The poet said:

Bakarat talumuka ba'da wahnin fi al-nadā / basl 'alayki malamati wa-'itabi

That is: forbidden to you.

In His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if she offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from her﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that if she ransoms with every ransom in terms of wealth and riches, said by Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

The second: in terms of Islam and repentance, said by al-Hasan.

Scholars differed on whether it is abrogated, with two opinions. The first: it is abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [At-Tawbah: 5], said by Qatadah.

The second: it remains in force as a warning, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [Al-Muddaththir: 11], said by Mujahid.

"Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us?" That is, the idols. Regarding calling upon them in this context, there are two interpretations. One: worshipping them. The second: seeking success from them.

If it is said: How does He say "nor harm us"? Is calling upon them not harmful, since it makes one deserving of punishment? It is said: its meaning is "that which does not possess for us any harm or benefit."

﴿And be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us﴾ to Islam.

﴿Like one whom the devils have enticed into the earth﴾. In this there are two statements. One: that it is their summoning to their aim and their following, like His saying: ﴿So make hearts of people incline toward them﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], meaning they aim at them and follow them. The second: that they command him by desire.

Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and his wife when they called their son 'Abd al-Rahman to Islam and guidance, that he should come to them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾. Regarding the truth by which He created the heavens and the earth, there are four opinions. The first: that it is wisdom. The second: kindness to the servants. The third: the very act of creating them, for it is true. (p-133) The fourth: that it means by the word of truth.

﴿And the day He says, "Be," and it is﴾. In this there are two statements. One: that He will say to the Day of Resurrection, "Be," and it will be; He does not repeat the word time after time. This was said by Muqatil. The second: that He says to the heavens, "Become a trumpet," which will be blown for the establishment of the Hour, so they become a trumpet like the Qur'an, and another heaven is substituted. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And His is the dominion on the day the trumpet is blown﴾, there are two statements. One: that the trumpet is a horn blown into; the first blast is for annihilation, and the second for resurrection, as a sign of the ending and the beginning. This is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall dead, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown again, and immediately they will be standing, looking on﴾ [Az-Zumar: 68]. The second: that the trumpet is the plural of ṣūrah (form), into which its spirit will be blown, and they will live.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. In this there are two statements. One: that it refers to the creation of the heavens and the earth; the unseen is what is hidden from you, and the witnessed is what you witness. The second: that it refers to the blowing of the trumpet; He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the one who manages the blast.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 74–79:**

Allah's words: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾. On this there are three opinions.

The first: Azar is the name of his father. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Muhammad said: he was a man from Kuthā, a village in the district of Kufa.

The second: Azar is the name of an idol, and the name of his father was Tarih. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: it is not a proper name but a descriptive epithet of reproach with a defect, and its meaning is "crooked," as if he were faulting him for his deviation from the truth. This is the view of al-Farra'.

If it is asked: how is it valid for Abraham, who was a prophet, to revile his father? It is answered: he reviled him for neglecting the right of Allah, the Exalted, and the right of a parent falls away when one neglects the right of Allah.

(p-135) Allah's words: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth﴾. The words *dhālika*, *dhāka* and *dhā* are demonstratives. However, *dhā* is used for what is near, *dhālika* for what is far, and *dhāka* to magnify the status of what is far.

Regarding the meaning of "the dominion of the heavens and the earth," there are five views. The first: it means that He created the heavens and the earth. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: it means the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth. Those who held this view differed on it in two ways. The first: *malakut* is *mulk* (sovereignty) in the Nabatean language. This is the view of Mujahid. The second: it is *mulk* in Arabic. It is said *mulk* and *malakut*, just as it is said *rahbah* and *rahabut*, and *rahmah* and *rahamut*. The Arabs say: *rahabut khayrin min rahamut*, meaning that being feared is better than being shown mercy. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The third: its meaning is the signs of the heavens and the earth. This is the view of Muqatil.

The fourth: it is the sun, the moon and the stars. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

The fifth: the dominion of the heavens is the moon, the stars and the sun, and the dominion of the earth is the mountains, the trees and the seas. This is the view of Qatadah.

﴿and that he might be among those who have certainty﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: among those who have certainty of the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted, and of His power.

﴿He said: "I do not love those that set."﴾ He means love of a lord who is worshipped. Otherwise there is no harm in loving them, apart from loving the Lord.

﴿When he saw the moon rising﴾, i.e., ascending. Likewise *bazghat al-shams* means the sun rose.

If it is asked: why was its setting evidence that it is not permissible to worship it, when a group of intelligent people worshipped it despite knowing it sets? It is answered: because its change by setting is evidence that it is governed and created, and whatever has this attribute cannot be a god who is worshipped.

The commentary of the verse: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾. Regarding the wrongdoing (*zulm*) here, there are two opinions. The first is that it is polytheism (*shirk*), as said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn Mas'ud narrated: "When this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily on the Muslims, and they said: 'None of us is there but that he wrongs himself.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is not as you think; rather, it is as Luqman said to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate others with Allah. Indeed, association is a great wrongdoing﴾ [Luqman: 13].'" The second opinion is that it refers to all kinds of wrongdoing.

Those who hold this view differ over whether the term is general or specific, in two opinions. The first is that it is general. The second is that it is specific.

Those who hold that it is specific differ over who it was revealed about, in two opinions. The first is that this verse was revealed about Abraham specifically, and that this community has no share in it, as said by Ali, may Allah honour his face. The second is that it concerns those who emigrated to Medina, as said by Ikrimah.

They differ also over who this verse was the reply of, in three opinions. The first is that it is a reply from Allah, the Exalted, by which He separated Abraham from those among his people who argued with him, as said by Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq. The second is that it is the reply of his people when he asked them: ﴿So which of the two parties has more right to security?﴾ and they answered with what served as proof against them, as said by Ibn Jurayj. The third is that it is Abraham's own reply, as a scholar asks himself and then answers himself, related by al-Zajjaj.

The commentary of the verse: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people﴾. Regarding this argument with which he was endowed, there are three opinions. The first is his saying to them: ﴿Do you worship besides Allah that which can neither harm nor benefit you? Or do you worship He who holds the power of harm and benefit?﴾ They said: "The Lord of harm and benefit has more right [to be worshipped]." The second is that when he said: ﴿So which of the two parties has more right to security?﴾ [meaning:] "the worship of one God, or of many gods?" They said: "The worship of one God," and so they acknowledged this against themselves. The third is that when they said to Abraham: "Do you not fear that our gods will afflict you with madness?" he said: "Do you not fear that your gods will afflict you, by your joining the small with the great in worship?"

They differ over the cause of the argument becoming manifest to Abraham, in two opinions. The first is that Allah, the Exalted, put it into his mind until he extracted it by his own reflection. The second is that He commanded him with it and inspired it to him.

The commentary of: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾. Regarding it there are four aspects. The first: with Allah, by attaining knowledge of Him. The second: in rank among creation, by being chosen for His message. The third: by generosity. The fourth: by good character.

In it there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*), and its intended sense is: "We raise by degrees whom We will."

"His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying: ﴿If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted with them a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. Concerning them there are five opinions.

The first: "If Quraysh disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted with them the Helpers (al-Ansar)." This is the view of al-Dahhak.

The second: "If the people of Makkah disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted with them the people of Madinah." This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The third: "If Quraysh disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted with them the angels." This is the view of Abu Raja'.

The fourth: that they are the eighteen prophets whom Allah mentioned earlier with His saying: ﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob﴾. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The fifth: that they are all the believers. This is the view of some of the later scholars.

As for His saying: ﴿then We have entrusted with them﴾, its meaning is: We have appointed (aqamna) to guard them and to support them, meaning: the books of Allah and the law of His religion.(p-141)

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 91–92:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations:

First: They did not magnify Him with His true magnificence. This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri), al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

Second: They did not know Him with His true knowledge. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

Third: They did not describe Him with His true description. This was said by al-Khalil.

Fourth: They did not believe that God has power over everything. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿When they said: God did not send down anything to a human being﴾, meaning, a Book from heaven.

Regarding this Book, whose revelation they denied, there are two opinions. The first is that it is the Torah. A Jewish rabbi (hibr) denied what was revealed in it, according to a report that "the Prophet (ﷺ) saw this Jewish rabbi to be fat, and said to him: 'Do you not read in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?' He became angry at this and said: God did not send down anything to a human being. The Jews then disowned him and cursed him." This was related by Ibn Bahr.

The second opinion is that it is the Qur'an, which they denied, rejecting that the Qur'an was sent down.

Regarding the one who said this there are two opinions: the first is the Quraysh; the second is the Jews.

God therefore answered them with His saying: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book that Moses brought﴾, meaning the Torah, because they acknowledged its revelation.

(p-142) Then He said: ﴿as a light and guidance for the people﴾, because what is sent down from heaven can only be a light and guidance.

Then He said: ﴿you make it into scrolls, displaying them and concealing much﴾, meaning that they conceal what is in their Book about the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), his description, and the truth of his message.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down﴾, meaning the Qur'an. Regarding (mubarak, "blessed") there are three aspects. The first: it is greatly blessed because of the citing of it as evidence. The second: because of the increase in clarification it contains, since barakah is increase. The third: that mubarak means established and enduring.

﴿confirming what was before it﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: the earlier books, the Torah, the Gospel and others. This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri. The second: the second creation (al-nash'ah al-thaniyah), said by Ali ibn 'Isa.

﴿that you may warn the Mother of Cities﴾, meaning the people of the Mother of Cities, so the mention of "people" is omitted for brevity, as He said: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. The "Mother of Cities" is Mecca. Regarding why it is so named there are four sayings. The first: because it is the gathering place of the cities, just as children gather around the mother. The second: because the first house was established in it, so the cities are as if they grew out of it; this was said by al-Suddi. The third: because it is honored as a mother is honored; this was said by al-Zajjaj. The fourth: because people come to it from every side, that is, they make for it.

Then He said: ﴿and those around it﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the people of the whole earth.

(p-143) ﴿And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it﴾. Regarding what this pronoun refers back to, there are two opinions. The first: to the Book, the meaning being: those who believe in the Hereafter believe in this Book; this was said by al-Kalbi. The second: to Muhammad (ﷺ), the meaning being: those who believe in the Hereafter believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), because of the miracle God has manifested through him and the truthfulness God has shown in him; this was said by al-Farra'.

If it is said: what of the People of the Book who believe in the Hereafter but do not believe in it? It is answered: their belief in the Hereafter is not taken into account, because of their shortcoming in its due rights, so they are in the position of one who does not believe in it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 93–94:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him?﴾ There are two opinions about the one concerning whom this was revealed:

One: that it is Musaylima the Liar. This is the view of ʿIkrima.

The second: Musaylima and al-ʿAnsi. This is the view of Qatada.

Maʿmar has narrated from al-Zuhri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While I was sleeping, I saw that (p-144) in my two hands were two gold bracelets, and they weighed heavily upon me. Then it was revealed to me that I should blow on them, so I blew, and they flew away. I interpreted that as the two liars: the Liar of Yamama and the Liar of Sanaa, al-ʿAnsi."

﴿And who says, "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed"?﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions:

One: those already mentioned who claimed revelation and prophethood.

The second: that it is ʿAbdullah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh. This is the view of al-Suddi. Al-Farra' said: "He used to write for the Prophet (ﷺ). When the Prophet said, ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾, he would write ﴿Hearing, Knowing﴾ and ﴿Mighty, Wise﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) would say to him, 'Both are the same,' until he dictated to him: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ up to His words: ﴿another creation﴾. The third: what al-Hakam related from ʿIkrima: that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, because he imitated the Qur'an, saying: "By the grinders, grinding; by the kneaders, kneading; by the bakers, baking; by the morsels, morseling."

Concerning His saying: ﴿And the angels stretch forth their hands﴾ there are two opinions:

One: "stretching forth their hands" with punishment. This is the view of al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

The second: stretching forth their hands to seize the souls from the bodies. This is the view of al-Farra'.

It is also possible, as a third meaning, that they stretch forth their hands with the scrolls of deeds.

﴿Bring forth your souls﴾ has two opinions:

One: from your bodies at the moment of witnessing death, as a humiliation and harshness upon them, even though the bringing forth of the soul is the act of others.

(p-145) The second: "Bring forth your souls from the punishment if you are able," as a rebuke and reproach to them for wronging themselves. This is the view of al-Hasan.

It is also possible, as a third meaning, that it means: "Save your souls by offering argument on their behalf concerning what you did."

﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation (al-hawn)﴾. Al-Hawn with a *damma* means humiliation, as said by Dhu al-Usba' al-ʿAdwani:

"I go to you, mother, with a shepherdess who pastures the young camels, and I will not shut my eyes upon humiliation (al-hawn)."

As for al-hawn with a *fatha*, it means gentleness, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾, meaning with gentleness and tranquility. The reciter said:

"Calm yourselves; time does not return what has passed; do not let yourselves perish in grief over one who has died."

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾. Furada means alone, and it may carry two meanings: one, alone without helpers; the second, alone without wealth.

﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾, meaning what We gave you as possessions. Al-takhwil is the granting of property. Abu al-Najm said:

"He gave and did not withhold, and he did not withhold; the lord of the heaps of wealth bestows upon whoever was bestowed upon."

﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings: one, their gods whom they used to worship, as said by al-Kalbi; the second, the angels whom they believed would intercede for them, as said by Muqatil.

(p-146) ﴿Those whom you claimed were partners among you﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings: one, meaning intercessors, as said by al-Kalbi; the second, meaning bearing burdens on your behalf as partners bear burdens for partners.

﴿Indeed, your bonds have been severed among you﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings: one, your assembly has dispersed in the Hereafter; the second, your ties of connection have vanished in this world, as said by Mujahid.

Whoever reads ﴿baynakum﴾ with a *fatha* means: the matter has been cut off among you.

﴿And lost from you is what you used to claim﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings: one, from the absence of resurrection and recompense; the second, from your intercessors before Allah.

If it is said: His saying, ﴿And you have come to Us﴾, is a report about the past, while the intended meaning is the future? There are two answers to this.

One: it is said to them this in the Hereafter, so it is, according to the apparent sense, a report.

The second: because its occurrence is certain, it is treated as if it had already happened, and so it is permissible, even though it is future, to express it in the past tense.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 95–97:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: it means the splitter of the grain from the ear (sunbulah) and of the date-stone from the palm tree. This was said by al-Hasan.

Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said likewise.

The second: that al-Falaq (splitting) is the cleft that is in them both. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: that it means the Creator of the grain and the date-stone. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Some of the people of subtle meanings (ashab al-ghawamid) mentioned a fourth opinion: that it means the One who brings forth what is in the heart's grain of sincerity and of showing off (riya').

﴿He brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: He brings forth the living ear from the dead grain, and the living palm tree from the dead date-stone; and by bringing forth the dead from the living is meant that He brings forth the dead grain from the living ear, and the dead date-stone from the living palm tree. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: that He brings forth the human being from the drop (nutfah), and the drop from the human being. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: He brings forth the believer from the disbeliever, and the disbeliever from the believer. This was said by al-Hasan.

We have also mentioned a possibility regarding this: that He brings forth the sharp, resolute one from the dull, incapable one, and brings forth the dull, incapable one from the sharp, resolute one.

﴿That is Allah; so how are you turned away?﴾ That is, you are turned away from the truth.

﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions. The first: the splitter of the dawn; this was said by Qatadah.

The second: that it is the brightening of dawn; this was said by Mujahid.

The third: that its meaning is the Creator of the light of day; this is the saying of al-Dahhak.

The fourth: that the dawn (al-isbah) is the sunlight by day and the moonlight by night; this was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿And He made the night a means of rest﴾. Regarding this there are two sayings: (p-148) One of them: it was named "rest" (sakan) because every creature that moves by day rests in it.

The second: because every living thing retreats in it to its dwelling.

﴿And the sun and the moon as a reckoning﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings. The first: its meaning is that they both run in their stations by calculation and proof; in it there is a beginning and a return to increase and decrease. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi.

The second: that is, He made them a means for knowing the reckoning of the months and years.

The third: that is, He made the sun and the moon a light (diya'); this was said by Qatadah, and he seems to have taken it from His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He sends upon it a reckoning from the sky﴾ [al-Kahf: 40], saying: "fire."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 98–99:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿It is He who produced you from a single soul﴾ — meaning Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿Then a lodging and a deposit﴾ — concerning this there are six interpretations. The first: "a lodging" in the earth and "a deposit" in the loins (al-aslab), related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "a lodging" in the womb and "a deposit" in the grave, related by Ibn Masʿud.

The third: "a lodging" in the wombs of women and "a deposit" in the loins of men, related by ʿAta and Qatada.

(p-149) The fourth: "a lodging" in this world and "a deposit" in the Hereafter, related by Mujahid.

The fifth: "a lodging" on the earth and "a deposit" in the grave, related by al-Hasan.

The sixth: that the "lodging" is what has been created, and the "deposit" is what has not yet been created; this is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky, and by it We bring forth the vegetation of every thing﴾ — concerning this there are two views. The first: its meaning is the provision of every living thing among the animals.

The second: the vegetation of every thing among the fruits.

﴿Then We bring forth from it green (shoots)﴾ — meaning a moist crop, in contrast to its state when it was sown.

﴿We bring forth from it grain arranged in layers﴾ — meaning the ear of grain whose kernels are layered upon one another.

﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters hanging low﴾ — qinwan is the plural of qinw (a cluster), and concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: that it is the spathe (al-tal', the sheath of the flower), related by al-Dahhak.

The second: that it is the central stalk (al-jimar).

The third: that they are the strands (al-a'dhaq), as Imru' al-Qays said:

؎ Its upper parts became heavy and its roots were overturned, and it inclined with clusters of unripe dates, reddish.

﴿hanging low﴾ — concerning this there are two views. The first: they hang low for the one who gathers them, because the palm is short and its fruit is easy to reach, related by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: some of them are close to others because they are near one another, related by al-Hasan.

﴿And gardens of grapevines﴾ — meaning orchards of grapevines.

﴿Olive-like and unlike﴾ — concerning this there are two views. The first: they resemble one another in their leaves while their fruit differs, related by Qatada.

The second: they resemble one another in colour while their taste differs, related by al-Kalbi.

﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit﴾ — Hamza and al-Kisa'i read thamarihi (with a ḍamma on the thā' and mīm, as thumurihi), while the rest read thamarihi with a fatḥa. Concerning this difference between the ḍamma and the fatḥa there are two views. The first: thumur with a ḍamma is the plural of thimar (fruits), and with a fatḥa it is the plural of thamara (a single fruit), related by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

The second: thumur with a ḍamma means property, and with a fatḥa means the fruit of the palm, related by Mujahid and Abu Jaʿfar al-Tabari.

﴿And its ripening﴾ — meaning its maturity and its reaching completion.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 100:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Yet they make the jinn partners with God, though He created them﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions.

The first: the Magians attributed evil to Iblis (Satan), and by this they made him a partner of God.

The second: the polytheists of the Arabs made the angels daughters of God and His partners. This was said by Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd, in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship, but the jinn know that they will be brought forth [for judgment]﴾. He named the angels "jinn" because they are hidden from the eyes.

The third: they obeyed Satan in the worship of idols until they made them partners of God in worship. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj.

﴿Though He created them﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: He created them without any partner [with Him], so why did they make a partner for Him in worship? The second: He created those whom they made partners, so how could they become partners in worship?

Yahya ibn Ya'mur read (wa-khalqahum) with the lam (ل) pronounced with a sukun (ـْ).

Its meaning is that they made the idols, which they fashioned with their own hands, partners of God.

﴿And they attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge﴾. Regarding (kharaqu) there are two readings, with light and with heavy emphasis (tashdid). Concerning it there are two opinions. The first: the meaning of (kharaqu) is "they lied," said by Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Juraij, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: its meaning is "they created for Him sons and daughters," and (al-khalq) and (al-kharq) are one, said by al-Farra'.

The second opinion: the meanings of the two readings differ. Regarding their difference there are two views. The first: the form with tashdid indicates intensification. The second: the form without tashdid means "they lied," and the form with tashdid means "they disagreed."

"Sons" refers to the saying of the Christians about the Messiah that he is the son of God, and the saying of the Jews that Uzayr is the son of God.

"Daughters" refers to the saying of the polytheists of the Arabs about the angels that they are the daughters of God.

﴿Without knowledge﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: without knowledge from them that He has sons and daughters. The second: without any proof indicating to them that He has sons and daughters.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 101–103:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision﴾. Concerning this, the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) have five opinions.

(p-152) The first: its meaning is that sights cannot encompass Him, and He encompasses sights. The proponent of this view argued with His saying: ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾. Here God described drowning (al-gharaq) as having "overtaken" (adraka) Pharaoh, and drowning is not described as seeing. Likewise, the "overtaking" (idrak) here does not preclude seeing with sight, though this wording does not necessitate it, even if His saying indicates it: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [75:22–23].

The second opinion: its meaning is that sights do not see Him, and He sees sights. Those who held this view argued on two grounds. The first: sights perceive what is between them and not what is adjacent to them, and between the eye and what it sees there must necessarily be empty space. So if sights saw Him, He would be bounded and a place would be empty of Him, and these are the attributes of bodies which admit increase and decrease.

The second: sights perceive colors just as hearing perceives sounds. Thus, since He cannot be colored, He cannot be seen, just as whatever cannot have a sound cannot be heard.

The third opinion: the sights of creation do not perceive Him in this world, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾, and they perceive Him in the Hereafter, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿looking toward their Lord﴾ [75:23]; and He perceives sights in this world and the Hereafter.

The fourth: the sights of the wrongdoers do not perceive Him in this world or the Hereafter, while the sights of the believers do perceive Him; and He perceives sights in this world and the Hereafter, because perception of Him is an honor which is withheld from the people of sins.

(p-153) The fifth opinion: sights do not perceive Him in this world or the Hereafter, but God creates for His friends (awliya') a sixth sense beyond their five senses by which they see Him. They argue that God has informed us of their seeing Him; so if it is permissible that He be seen in the Hereafter with these eyes, even if their powers are increased, it is permissible that He be seen with them in this world, even if their powers are weakened, by a lesser degree than the vision of the Hereafter. For what is created for perceiving something is not deprived of perceiving it; rather, perception varies according to differences in strength and weakness. Since this (weakness) prevents perception, and God Most High has informed us of His perceiving them, it follows that what He informed us of is true and cannot be repelled by doubt, and that is by creating another sense through which perception occurs.

Then He said: ﴿And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾. This admits of two interpretations: The first: He is subtle (latif) toward His servants in bestowing favors upon them, and all-aware (khabir) of their welfare.

The second: He is subtle in governance (tadbir) and all-aware of wisdom (hikma).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 104–105:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Thus We vary the verses﴾. In this there are three aspects. The first: that some of it follows others, so the revelation is not interrupted.

The second: that the verse turns to various meanings, as an exaggeration of its inimitability (i'jaz) and as a distinction from the speech of humankind.

The third: that it is the variation in what it contains of promise and threat, command and prohibition, so that it is more forceful in admonition, more apt to bring about compliance, and more comprehensive of the public interest.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿and so they say, "You have studied"﴾. In the speech there is an elision, and its estimated meaning is: "lest they say, 'You have studied'." That was omitted for brevity, as in His saying, exalted: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176], meaning: lest you go astray.

In ﴿darasta﴾ there are five readings, whose interpretation differs according to their variation:

The first: (darasta), meaning "you have read and learned." Quraysh say this to the Prophet (ﷺ). This was reported by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, and it is the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i.

The second: (darasta), meaning "you have studied with others and reviewed together." This was said by Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr.

In this reading there is a second interpretation: that it means "you disputed and argued."

The third: (darasat) with the ta' sukun, meaning "it has been effaced and has grown old." This was said by Ibn al-Zubayr and al-Hasan, and it is the reading of Ibn 'Amir.

The fourth: (duris) with a damma on the dal, the passive form, meaning "it has been recited and read." This was said by Qatadah.

The fifth: (daras), meaning "the Prophet (ﷺ) read and recited." This is the reading in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿and that We may make it clear to a people who know﴾ admits of two meanings: first, "to a people who understand (ya'qiluna)."

Second: "who know the aspects of clarification, even if they do not know the one who clarifies."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 106–108:

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And do not revile those who call upon other than Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge﴾. He means transgression (i'tida'). The people of Mecca read ʿadwan (ﻋَدُوًّا) with the shadda, meaning that they took Him as an enemy (ʿaduww).

On this there are two opinions. The first: Do not revile the idols, lest the worshippers of idols revile the one who reviles them. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: Do not revile them, lest anger and ignorance lead them to revile the One you worship, just as you reviled what they worship.

﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community its deeds﴾. On this there are three sayings. The first: Just as We made attractive to you the doing of the acts of obedience that We commanded you, so We made attractive to the believers who came before you the doing of the acts of obedience that We commanded them. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: Thus We made the deeds of every religious community appear to them as dubious matters (shubuhat), as a trial for them, until their desires led them to these and they became blind to right guidance concerning them.

The third: Just as We made clear to you the proofs that indicate the truth, so We made clear to those before you proofs of the truth like those We made clear to you.

The Exalted and Glorified said: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it.﴾ These were a group of the polytheists of Makkah who swore by Allah to His Messenger (ﷺ) that if a sign they proposed came to them, they would surely believe in it. Ibn Juraij said: "They were the mockers."

Scholars differed about the sign they proposed, in three opinions: (p-156) The first: that He turn al-Safa into gold for us.

The second: what Allah mentioned at the end of: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ ﴿or you have a garden of palms and grapes and cause rivers to gush forth within it in abundance﴾ ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments, as you claim﴾, up to His words: ﴿a book we can read﴾. So when they swore to him, Allah commanded His Prophet to say to them: ﴿Say, the signs are only with Allah﴾.

The third: when His statement, may He be exalted, in ash-Shu'ara' was revealed: ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the sky, and their necks would remain bowed before it﴾, the polytheists said: "Send it down upon us until we believe in it, if you are of the truthful." The believers said: "O Messenger of Allah, send it down upon them so that they may believe." Then Allah revealed this verse. This was related by al-Kalbi.

It is not obligatory upon Allah to grant them what they propose, especially when He knows that they will not believe in it. Scholars differed on whether it is obligatory for Him if He knows they would believe in it, on two views. He has informed that they will not believe, by His statement: ﴿And what will make you aware that when it comes, they will not believe?﴾ Then the Exalted said: ﴿And We will turn their hearts and their sights away, just as they did not believe in it the first time﴾. This is a punishment from Allah upon them, and in it are three opinions: The first: that it is a punishment from Allah in the Hereafter, by which He turns them over in the Fire.

The second: in this world, by bewilderment, until it disturbs and distresses the soul.

The third: its meaning is that We encompass what the breasts conceal and the treachery of the eyes among them.

Regarding His statement: ﴿the first time﴾, there are two interpretations: The first: the first time the signs came to them.

The second: that "the first" refers to their states in this world entirely, and then Allah emphasized their state of confusion.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 111:

(p-157) He said: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered against them every thing face to face, they would not have believed﴾. In it there are two readings. The first: (qiblan) with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', recited by Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir. Its meaning is "by direct sight" (mu'ayanah) and "openly" (mujaharah). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The second reading: with a damma on the qaf and the ba', which is the reading of the rest of the Qurra'. In its interpretation there are three views. The first: qubul is the plural of qabil, meaning guarantor (kafil), so the meaning of (qubulan) is "as guarantors" (kufala').

The second: its meaning is "tribe by tribe and row by row" (qabilah qabilah wa saffan saffan). This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: its meaning is "in confrontation" (muqabalah). This is the view of Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq.

Then He said: ﴿They would not have believed﴾, meaning: with these signs, even though they had proposed them earlier.

Then He said: ﴿Unless Allah wills﴾. In it there are two views. The first: that He would help them to it. The second: unless He wills to compel them to it. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

Then He said: ﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾. In it there are two aspects. The first: they are ignorant regarding the signs they propose. The second: they are ignorant that, even if their proposals were granted, they would not believe willingly.

And so We have appointed for every prophet an enemy — devils of mankind and jinn — Hmm, I must translate exactly.

"His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy﴾ — meaning: We have made for the prophets enemies, just as We made for other people enemies among mankind.

In ﴿We have made﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that We decreed that they are enemies. The second: its meaning is that We left them upon enmity, and did not prevent them from it.

In ﴿devils of mankind and jinn﴾ there are three opinions. The first: it means the devils of mankind who are with mankind, and the devils of the jinn who are with the jinn; this was said by ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi.

The second: the devils of mankind are their disbelievers, and the devils of the jinn are their disbelievers; this was said by Mujahid.

The third: that the devils of mankind and jinn are their rebellious ones (marada); this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

﴿Some of them inspire to others﴾ — in "yuhi" (inspire) there are three aspects. The first: it means some of them whisper to others.

The second: some of them gesture to others, and he expressed the gesture by "revelation" (wahy), as in His saying: ﴿So He revealed to them to glorify [Him] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 11]. And ﴿the adorned speech﴾ is what they embellished for them of doubts in disbelief and committing sins.

The third: some of them command others, as in His saying: ﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾ [Fussilat: 12], meaning its command.

Then He said: ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾ — this admits two meanings. The first: they would not have done the disbelief. The second: they would not have done the adorned speech.

Regarding their being left to that, there are two opinions. The first: as a trial for them and a distinction of the believers from them. The second: He does not compel them to faith, for then obligation (taklif) would cease.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾ — meaning: their hearts incline toward it. Al-iṣghāʾ (inclining) is al-mayl (inclination). The poet said:

You see the fool, because of him, turning away from every clear ruling, and in him is an inclination toward the ambiguous.

The sense of the speech is: some of them inspire to others adorned speech as delusion, so that they may deceive them, and so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it. Some people said: rather, it is the lam of command, and its meaning is informative.

﴿And that they may be pleased with it﴾ — because whoever's heart inclines toward something is pleased with it, even if it is not pleasing.

The second: some of them gesture to others, and he expressed the gesture by "revelation" (wahy), as in His saying: ﴿So He revealed to them to glorify [Him] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 11]. And ﴿the adorned speech﴾ is what they embellished for them of doubts in disbelief and committing sins.

The third: some of them command others, as in His saying: ﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾ [Fussilat: 12], meaning its command.

Then He said: ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾ — this admits two meanings. The first: they would not have done the disbelief. The second: they would not have done the adorned speech.

Regarding their being left to that, there are two opinions. The first: as a trial for them and a distinction of the believers from them. The second: He does not compel them to faith, for then obligation (taklif) would cease.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾ — meaning: their hearts incline toward it. Al-iṣghāʾ (inclining) is al-mayl (inclination). The poet said:

You see the fool, because of him, turning away from every clear ruling, and in him is an inclination toward the ambiguous.

The sense of the speech is: some of them inspire to others adorned speech as delusion, so that they may deceive them, and so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it. Some people said: rather, it is the lam of command, and its meaning is informative.

﴿And that they may be pleased with it﴾ — because whoever's heart inclines toward something is pleased with it, even if it is not pleasing.

﴿And that they may earn what they are earning﴾ — in it there are two interpretations. The first: that they may acquire of shirk and sins what they are acquiring; this was said by Juwaybir. The second: that they may lie against Allah and His Messenger what they are lying; and this is a possibility.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God?﴾ There are two interpretations of this. The first: its meaning is, "Is it permissible for anyone to deviate from God's judgment, so that I would deviate from it?"

The second: "Is it permissible for anyone to judge alongside God, so that I would appeal to him?"

The difference between *hakam* (an arbiter, one fit to judge) and *hakim* (a judge) is that the *hakam* is the one who is qualified for judgment, so he does not judge except with truth, whereas the *hakim* may be someone not qualified for it, who judges without truth. Thus *hakam* is one of the attributes of His essence, and *hakim* is one of the attributes of His action. Therefore *hakam* is more emphatic in praise than *hakim*.

(p-160) Then He said: ﴿And it is He who has sent down to you the Book, detailed.﴾ Regarding "detailed" (*mufassal*) there are four interpretations. The first: the detailing of its verses to clarify their meanings, so that they are not obscure.

The second: the distinguishing of the truthful from the false.

The third: the distinguishing of truth from falsehood and guidance from misguidance; this is the view of al-Hasan.

The fourth: the distinguishing of command from prohibition, the recommended from the forbidden, and the lawful from the unlawful.

The occasion of revelation of this verse: the polytheists of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Appoint between us and you an arbiter, if you wish, from the rabbis (*ahbar*) of the Jews, or if you wish, from the rabbis of the Christians, so that he may inform us about you from what is in their Book concerning your affair." So this verse was revealed to him.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.﴾ This means the Qur'an. Regarding its fulfillment there are four possible interpretations. The first: the completeness of its proofs and evidences.

The second: the completeness of its rulings and commands.

The third: the completeness of its warning through promise and threat.

The fourth: the completeness of its speech and the perfection of its forms.

Regarding His words ﴿in truth and justice﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: truthful in its promise and its threat, and just in its commands and prohibitions; this was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: truthful in what it reports, and just in what it decrees; this is the meaning of the view of Qatadah.

The interpretation of ﴿None can alter His words﴾ has already passed.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 116–120:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Leave alone the outward and the inward of sin﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations:

The first: its outward and its inward are its open and its secret [aspects]. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: the outward of sin is what has been forbidden of marrying those within the prohibited degrees, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾, to the end of the verse. And its inward is adultery (zina). This is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: that the outward of sin is the women who take flags (openly practising prostitution), and the inward is those who take lovers (akhdan), because they used to consider it lawful in secret. This is related from al-Suddi and al-Dahhak.

The fourth: that the outward of sin is nakedness (al-'urya), which they practised when they circumambulated the House naked, and its inward is adultery. This is related from Ibn Zayd.

It may also be held, as a fifth [interpretation], that the outward of sin is what one does with the limbs, and its inward is what one believes in the heart.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 121:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: what is meant is slaughtered animals which the Arabs used to slaughter for their idols; this is the view of ʿAṭāʾ.

The second: it refers to carrion (al-maytah), this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

The third: it refers to the game of the polytheists who do not mention the name of Allah and are not among the people of invoking the name; it is forbidden for the Muslims to eat it unless they themselves are the ones who hunted it. This is related by Ibn Baḥr.

(p-162) The fourth: it refers to whatever over which Allah's name was not mentioned at the time of its slaughter.

Concerning the prohibition of eating it there are three opinions. The first: it is not forbidden [whether] one leaves out the mention [of Allah's name] intentionally or forgetfully; this is the view of al-Ḥasan and al-Shāfiʿī.

The second: it is forbidden if one leaves it out intentionally, and not forbidden if one leaves it out forgetfully; this is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah.

The third: it is forbidden whether one leaves it out intentionally or forgetfully; this is the view of Ibn Sīrīn and Dāwūd.

﴿And indeed it is certainly defiance (fisq)﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One: what is meant by it is disobedience; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: what is meant by it is sin (ithm).

﴿And indeed the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you﴾. He means disputing about the slaughtered animal. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: by "the devils" he meant a people from among the Persians who wrote to their allies among the Quraysh that Muḥammad and his companions claim that they follow the command of Allah, yet they do not eat what Allah has slaughtered, meaning carrion, and they eat what they themselves slaughter. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse concerning them; this is the view of ʿIkrimah.

The second: that the devils said this to their allies among the Quraysh; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

The third: that a people from among the Jews said this to the Prophet (ﷺ); this is related from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Regarding their "inspiring" to them there are two meanings. One: it is their signalling (ishāratuhum). The second: it is their message (risālatuhum).

﴿And if you obey them, indeed you are certainly polytheists﴾. He means in eating carrion; indeed you are polytheists if you deem it lawful.

(p-163) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Or one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ has three interpretations. The first: he was dead when he was a drop of semen (nutfah), and We gave him life by breathing the spirit into him. This is related from Ibn Bahr.

The second: he was dead through disbelief, and We gave him life by guiding him to faith. This is related from Ibn Isa.

The third: he was dead through ignorance, and We gave him life through action. Some of the scholars recited to me, as evidence for the soundness of this interpretation, lines by one of the poets of Basra:

*In ignorance, before death, is a death for its people, and their bodies before the graves are graves.*
*Whoever has not been given life by knowledge is dead, and for him there is no resurrection (nushur) before the true resurrection.*

﴿And We made for him a light by which he walks among the people﴾ has three opinions. The first: the light is the Qur'an, as said by al-Hasan.

The second: it is the knowledge that guides to right conduct (rushd).

The third: it is the goodness of faith.

His saying ﴿by which he walks among the people﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: he spreads by it the remembrance of his religion among the people in this world, until he becomes like one who walks [openly among them].

The second: he is guided by it among the people to Paradise, so he is the one who walks [on the path].

﴿Is one whose likeness is in the darkness, from which he cannot come out?﴾ has two opinions. The first: the darknesses are disbelief.

The second: they are ignorance. He compared it to darkness because its possessor is in bewilderment that leads him to ruin, like the bewilderment of one who walks in the dark.

The scholars differed concerning this verse according to two views.

The first: it is general, applying to every believer and every disbeliever. This is said by al-Hasan and others of the scholars.

The second: it is specific, referring to a particular individual.

Concerning the person to whom its revelation is specifically attributed, there are two views. The first: the believer is Umar ibn al-Khattab and the disbeliever is Abu Jahl. This is said by al-Dahhak.

And Muqatil [said the same].

(p-164) The second: the believer is Ammar ibn Yasir and the disbeliever is Abu Jahl. This is said by Ikrimah and al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 123–124:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And when a sign comes to them﴾ means a sign that indicates the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the soundness of his message.

﴿They say, "We will never believe"﴾ may have two meanings. One: "We will never believe in the sign." The second: "We will never believe in the Prophet (ﷺ)." ﴿Until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God﴾ may have two meanings. One: "the like of what the messengers of God were given of honour (karamah)."

The second: "the like of what they were given of prophethood (nubuwwah)."

﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ he intends by this two matters. One: the exclusivity of God Exalted in knowing the benefit (maslahah) concerning the one who deserves the message.

The second: a refutation of them for asking for what they do not deserve, and a prohibition against what it is not permissible for them to ask.

﴿Humiliation from God will befall those who committed crime﴾. Al-sagar (humiliation) is abasement; it is called sagar because a person belittles himself (yasghuru ila al-insan nafsahu).

Regarding His saying, ﴿from God﴾, there are three interpretations. One: "from God," so the word "min" (from) is omitted for brevity (ijaz).

The second: their refusal to follow the truth is humiliation in God's sight and abasement, if it is in them arrogance and pride; this was said by al-Farra'.

The third: humiliation in the Hereafter; this was said by al-Zajjaj.(p-165)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 125:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast for Islam﴾. There are two views on this. The first: He guides him to attaining reward and deserving honour.

The second: He guides him to the proofs that lead to the truth.

﴿He expands his breast for Islam﴾: the expansion of the breast means its widening to receive Islam and to let it firmly settle within it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ [al-Sharh 94:1]. Amr ibn Murrah narrated from Abu Ja'far, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked: Which of the believers is the most astute? He said: (The one who remembers death most and prepares best for what comes after it)." He said: "The Prophet ﷺ was asked about this verse. They said: How is the breast expanded, O Messenger of Allah? He said: (A light is cast into it, and it opens and expands.) They said: Is there a sign by which one may know this? He said: (Turning in repentance towards the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before the encounter with death)." Ibn Mas'ud narrated the like of this.

Then He said: ﴿And whomever He wills to lead astray﴾. There are two views on this. The first: He leads him astray from being guided to the truth.

The second: He leads him astray from attaining reward and deserving honour.

﴿He makes his breast tight, constricted﴾: meaning, tight, not allowing entry of Islam.

﴿Constricted (ḥarajan)﴾: there are three interpretations. The first: that it is extremely hard, so that nothing settles in it.

The second: that it is extremely narrow, so that nothing enters it.

The third: that its place is white (i.e., dense, closed, like a thicket that is not penetrated).

﴿As if he were climbing up into the sky﴾: there are four interpretations. The first: as if he were commanded to ascend to the sky, given its impossibility for him and its distance from him.

The second: as if he finds no path, because the paths are closed to him, except an ascent into the sky which he is unable to achieve.

The third: as if he is turned away from it, recoiling from it, rising up towards the sky.

The fourth: as if his heart ascends to the sky due to its hardship upon him and its difficulty for him.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus Allah places the abomination upon those who do not believe﴾. As for the rijs (abomination), there are five interpretations. The first: that it is that in which there is no good; this was said by Mujahid.

The second: that it is punishment; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: wrath; this was said by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: that it is Satan; this was said by Ibn Abbas.

The fifth: that rijs and najas are one and the same; this is the view of some of the grammarians of Kufa, and 'Ali ibn 'Isa related it.

Qatadah narrated from Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that when he entered the toilet he would say: (p-167) "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the abominations and the impurities, the male and female devils, the accursed Satan."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 126–127:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And this is the path of your Lord, straight﴾. We have mentioned that the ṣirāṭ (path) is the ṭarīq (road), and from it is the saying of ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl:

؎ We filled their land with horses until we left them more humbled than the ṣirāṭ (road)

Regarding it here there are two opinions. The first: he means that Islam is the straight path to God, most high. This was said by al-Kalbī.

The second: he means that the clear explanation (al-bayān) in the Qur'an is the straight path.

﴿We have detailed﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: We have made clear. The second: We have distinguished.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿For them is the abode of peace with their Lord﴾. This is Paradise. Regarding its being called the abode of peace there are two meanings. The first: because it is the abode of lasting safety from every calamity; this was said by al-Zajjāj. The second: that al-Salām is God, and Paradise is His abode, and therefore it is called the abode of peace; this is the meaning of the saying of al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī.

Regarding His saying ﴿with their Lord﴾ there are two meanings. The first: the abode of peace is with their Lord in the Hereafter, because it is most specific to Him. The second: its meaning is that for them, with their Lord, is that He will settle them in the abode of peace.

﴿And He is their Guardian because of what they used to do﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: He is their Helper in this world for their faith. The second: He is the One who undertakes their reward in the Hereafter for their deeds.(p-١٦٨)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 128:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And on the Day He will gather them all together﴾ means: He will gather the jinn and the humans all together on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿O assembly of jinn, you have taken much of mankind﴾ On this there are two views. The first: "you have taken much of them" in misguiding and leading them astray. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Mujahid.

The second: "you have taken much of mankind" by your misleading of them.

﴿And their allies among mankind will say: Our Lord, we benefited from one another﴾ On this there are three sayings. The first: its meaning is that some of us benefited from the companionship of others in cooperation and mutual support.

The second: some of us benefited from others in what they adorned for one another of following desires and committing sins.

The third: the benefit they derived from the jinn was what they were upon of seeking refuge with them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that there were men among mankind who sought refuge with men among the jinn﴾. This is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj.

Then, on this there are two aspects: the first: it is the benefit of mankind from the jinn. The second: it is the benefit of some of mankind from others.

And there is a third aspect on this: that mankind benefited from the jinn, and the jinn benefited from mankind, in their belief that they [the humans] could bring benefit.

﴿And we have reached our term which You appointed for us﴾ On this there are two views. The first: it is death. This is the view of al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The second: it is the gathering (al-hashr).

﴿He will say: The Fire is your abode﴾ i.e., the place of your dwelling, because al-mathwa (the abode) is residence. From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ Indeed he dwelt for a year, a sojourn he dwelt in, in which the she-camels are milked and the grazing herd grows weary.

(p-169) ﴿Abiding therein eternally, except what God wills﴾ Regarding "illa" (except) in this context there are three aspects. The first: it means "but" (lakin), as said by Sibawayh. The second: it means "other than" (siwa), as said by al-Farra'. The third: it is used in its literal sense, and this is the view of the majority.

And regarding this exception there are three sayings.

The first: the duration of the exception is the duration of the presentation (al-ʿarḍ) on the Day of Resurrection, which is the period between their being raised from their graves until their arrival at Hell. It is as if He said: "The Fire is your abode, abiding therein eternally, except for this period which He mentioned, for during it they are not abiding eternally in the Fire."

The second: its meaning is "abiding therein eternally, except what God wills" of renewing their skins after they are burned and of their being turned over to various kinds of punishment, or leaving them therein in their first state. So the exception concerns the attribute of the punishment, not the eternity of abiding in the Fire.

The third: He has made their affair regarding the extent and duration of their punishment subject to His will, exalted is He. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "No one should pass judgment upon God regarding His creation, nor does He place them in Paradise or in the Fire."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 129:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾. In this there are five interpretations.

The first: its meaning is, "And thus We leave some of them to others, so We do not help them, and whoever is deprived of God's help is destroyed."

The second: "And thus We make some of them an ally (wali) of others in disbelief."

The third: "And thus We make some of them suffer the punishment of others in the Fire."

The fourth: its meaning is that some of them follow others in the Fire, from al-muwalah (allegiance), which is following. This was said by Qatadah.

The fifth: the empowering of some of them over others through injustice and transgression. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 130:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind﴾. Al-ma'shar (assembly): the complete group of a people that comprises the various categories of groups. From this it is said of ten (ʿashara) that they are "the completion of the necklace" (tamam al-iqd).

﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses?﴾ The scholars differed regarding the sending of messengers to the jinn, in three opinions.

The first: that God sent messengers to the jinn from among them, just as He sent messengers to humankind from among them. This was said by al-Dahhak, and it is the apparent meaning of the speech.

The second: that God did not send messengers to them from among themselves; rather, messengers of humankind came to them. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. The plural in His saying ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you﴾ does not prevent the messengers from being from one of the two groups, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], whereas it emerges from only one of them.

The third: that the messengers of the jinn are those who, when they heard the Qur'an, ﴿turned back to their people as warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29]. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Regarding their entering Paradise there are two opinions. One of them was said by al-Dahhak.

(p-171) The second: that their reward is that they will be protected from the Fire, and then it will be said to them, "Be dust like the beasts." This was related by Sufyan from Layth.

﴿And they warned you of the meeting of this your day﴾. It may bear two meanings. One: they warned you of the abandonment of some of you by others and the disavowal of some of you from others on the Day of Resurrection.

The second: they warned you of what you would encounter therein of punishment for disbelief and retribution for sins.

﴿They said, "We bear witness against ourselves."﴾ It may bear two meanings. One: their acknowledgment against themselves that the messengers had warned them.

The second: the testimony of some of them against others regarding the messengers' warning to them.

﴿And the worldly life deceived them﴾. In this there are two meanings. (p-172) One: the adornment of the worldly life deceived them.

The second: leadership in the world deceived them.

It may also bear a third meaning: their life in the world deceived them, when they were given respite.

﴿And they bore witness against themselves﴾. In this testimony too are the two possible meanings, except that the former is testimony to the warning, and this is testimony to disbelief.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 131–132:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the cities unjustly while their people are unaware﴾. In this there are two interpretations.

The first: "Your Lord would not destroy the cities unjustly" on His part, but rather for a just cause that made them deserve destruction. This is the meaning of the statement of Muqatil.

The second: "Your Lord would not destroy the cities for the injustice of their people" until He has sent them warning, removed their excuses, and they have stepped out of the ruling of the unaware regarding what befalls them. This is the meaning of the statement of Mujahid.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they have done﴾. Its meaning: for every doer, whether of obedience to Allah or of disobedience to Him, there are degrees, i.e., ranks. They are called "degrees" (darajat) because of their differing, just as steps (daraj) differ in ascent and descent.

In this there are two interpretations. The first: that what is intended by them are the deeds, which differ in rank.

The second: that what is intended by them is the reward, which differs in rank.

This preference by degrees may be understood as applying to the people of Paradise and the people of Hellfire, because the people of Hellfire differ in punishment according to how they differ in evil deeds, just as the people of Paradise differ in reward according to how they differ in good deeds. However, the difference among the people of Paradise is sometimes expressed by "degrees" (darajat), and the difference among the people of Hellfire by "levels of descent" (darak). When the two are mentioned together in terms of difference, the difference of both is expressed by "degrees" (darajat), giving precedence to the description of the people of Paradise.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 133–135:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: O my people, act according to your standing﴾ — in it there are five interpretations.

The first: according to your way (ṭarīqa).

The second: according to your condition (ḥāla).

(p-173) The third: according to your side (nāḥiya), as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḥasan.

The fourth: according to your firm position (tamakkun), as said by al-Zajjaj.

The fifth: according to your stations (manāzil), as said by al-Kalbi.

﴿Indeed, I am acting﴾ — meaning: I warn you of the recompense of the one who obeys, which is reward, and of the one who disobeys, which is punishment.

﴿So you will come to know who will have the good outcome of the [final] abode﴾ — in it there are two interpretations. The first: you will come to know the reward of the Hereafter through faith and its punishment through disbelief, as an encouragement from Him toward its reward and a warning against its punishment.

The second: you will come to know God's victory in this world for His allies and His abandonment of His enemies, as said by Ibn Baḥr.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they assign to God a share of what He has created of the tilth and the cattle﴾. ﴿Of what He has created (mimma dhara'a)﴾ means "of what He has created," derived from "appearance" (al-zuhur). From it comes the saying "salt is dhurr," meaning because of its whiteness. It is also said that the white hair on the head is called dhur'a because of its becoming apparent. Al-harth (tilth) is crops, and al-an'am (cattle) are camels, cows and sheep; it is derived from the blessing (ni'mah) of mating.

This is a report from Him concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh and those who followed them among the polytheistic Arabs. They used to assign to God a share in their crops and livestock, and a share to their idols and images. God made their idols their "partners" (shuraka'uhum) because they had associated them in their wealth through the share they had assigned to them in it. Their share in the crops was a portion of them which they would designate for expenditure on those idols and their attendants.

Regarding their share from the cattle there are three opinions. The first: it is, like their share from the crops, designated for expenditure on those idols and their attendants. The second: it is an offering (qurban) to their idols, by which they drew near to them. The third: it refers to the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah, and the ham.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So what was for their partners does not reach God, and what was for God reaches their partners﴾. The interpreters differed about what is meant by this in four ways. The first: if something of what they had designated for their idols got mixed with their wealth, they returned it, and if what they had designated for God got mixed with it, they did not return it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: if what belonged to their idols was lost, they compensated for it, and if what belonged to God was lost, they did not compensate for it. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The third: they would spend some of what they had designated for God on their idols, but would not do the same with what they had designated for their idols. This was said by some of the later scholars.

The fourth: whatever they had designated for God from their slaughtered animals they would not eat until they had mentioned upon it the names of their idols, and they would not mention the name of God over what they had designated for their idols. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 137:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And thus their associates made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾. As for "their associates" here, there are four opinions concerning them. The first: they are the devils (shayatin), said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Suddi.

The second: they are people who used to serve the idols, said by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

The third: they are the misguided among the people.

Concerning what they made attractive to them of killing their children, there are two opinions. The first: one of them would swear that if he were blessed with such-and-such number of boys, he would slaughter one of them, just as ʿAbd al-Muttalib vowed concerning the slaughter of his son ʿAbd Allah, said by al-Kalbi.

The second: it is the burying of daughters alive out of fear of poverty, said by Mujahid.

﴿That they might ruin them﴾, meaning: that they might destroy them. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and his wealth will not avail him when he falls (tarrada)﴾ [al-Layl: 11], meaning when he perishes.

Concerning this there are two possibilities. The first: they intended by this to ruin them, just as they intended to lead them astray.

The second: they did not intend that, but it resulted in it, and so this is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), like His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], because its outcome became so, even though they did not intend it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 138:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And they say: These are cattle and tilth forbidden (ḥijr)﴾. That is, ḥijr means forbidden. From the same root is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: ḥijran maḥjūran﴾ [al-Furqan: 22], that is, forbidden. The poet said:

So I spent the night reclining, while my eye stays awake, as if my sleep upon the night were forbidden (maḥjūr).

﴿None may eat of them except whom we will, by their claim﴾. al-Kalbi said: they made them for men only, to the exclusion of women.

Regarding the cattle and the tilth of which they said that none may eat of them except whom they will, by their claim, there are two views.

One: that the cattle upon which they pass this ruling are, specifically, the baḥīra and the ḥām, and the tilth is what they set aside for their idols. This was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The second: that the cattle are the sacrificial animals of the idols, and the tilth is what they set aside for them.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And cattle whose backs are forbidden﴾. Regarding this there are two views: (p-176) One: that they are the sā'iba.

The second: that they are the ones over which they do not perform the Hajj, as said by Abu Wa'il.

﴿And cattle over which they do not mention the name of God﴾. These are the offerings of their idols: over them they mention the names of the idols, and they do not mention over them the name of God, exalted is He.

﴿Fabricating against Him﴾: that is, against God. Regarding this there are two views: One: that their attributing that to God is the fabrication against Him.

The second: that their mentioning the names of their idols at the slaughter in place of the name of God is the fabrication against Him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 139–140:

﴿They say: "What is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our wives."﴾ Al-A'mash read (khālişun) [in the masculine form]. Regarding ﴿khāliṣatun﴾ (feminine) and (khāliṣun) (masculine), there are two views. The first: ﴿khāliṣatun﴾ is more emphatic than (khāliṣun), even though it has the same meaning; the ta' marbuta was added for emphasis, as in their saying ʿallāmah (one who knows much) and nassābah (one who knows lineages). This was stated by al-Kisa'i.

The second: the addition of the ta' requires that it refer back to al-an'am (the livestock) because of its feminine gender, while omitting the ta' requires that it refer back to what is in their wombs because of its masculine gender. This was stated by al-Farra'.

On this there are three opinions. The first: what is in their wombs is the fetuses (al-ajinnah). This was stated by Mujahid.

The second: it is the milk (al-alban). This was stated by Qatadah.

The third (p-177): all of it, the fetuses and the milk. This was stated by Muqatil.

Regarding their assigning this to their males rather than to their females and wives, there are two views. The first: because the males are the servants of the idols (khuddam al-awthan).

The second: to give preference to males over females.

The word dhukur (males) derives from dhikr (mention). On its derivation from dhikr, there are two views. The first: because it is the one mentioned among people, so it is more prominent in mention than the female. 

The second: because it is more noble, and dhikr is nobility, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder (dhikr) for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44], meaning a source of honor.
