Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 141–142:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And it is He who produces gardens, both trellised and untrellised﴾. As for the jannat (gardens), they are the orchards surrounded by trees. As for the rawdah (meadow), it is the green land covered with vegetation. As for the zahrah (flowering land), it is the one with varied beautiful colours.

Regarding His saying ﴿trellised﴾ there are four opinions. The first: it refers to people trellising vines and others, by raising their branches. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

The second: its trellising is the raising of its fences and walls.

The third: they are those raised above the ground because of the height of their trees, so that their fruit does not fall on the ground. This is because the root of the word is elevation, and for this reason a throne (sarir) is called 'arsh because of its height. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿fallen upon its trellises﴾ [al-Kahf 42] and [al-Hajj 45], meaning upon their tops and what rose from them.

The fourth: the trellised ones are those trellised by people, and the untrellised ones are those that grew in the wilderness and the mountains.

﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾. The mention of eating was placed first for two reasons. The first: to facilitate giving its due. The second: to give precedence to their right and to begin with their benefit from their wealth.

Regarding His saying ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ there are three opinions. The first: it is the obligatory charity due on it: a tenth on what is watered without a device, and half a tenth on what is watered with a device. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it is a charity other than the zakat, obligatory on the day of harvest and gathering, and it is feeding those present and leaving what falls from the crop and the fruit. This was said by 'Ata' and Mujahid.

The third: this was obligatory before zakat and then abrogated (naskh) by it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Ibrahim.

﴿And do not be wasteful; indeed, He does not love the wasteful﴾. Concerning this there are five opinions. The first: this forbidden extravagance is that the owner of the property exceeds the amount obligatory upon him to an excess that burdens him. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Jurayj.

Sa'd ibn Sinan narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who exceeds the limit in charity is like the one who withholds it." And it was said: it was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, who gave away all of his produce until nothing remained in it that he could eat.

The second: it is that the ruler takes from him above what is obligatory upon him. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: it is that the owner of the property prevents the giving of the amount obligatory upon him. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The fourth: the intended extravagance is what they used to associate with their idols of tilled land and livestock. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The fifth: it is that one is extravagant in eating from them before paying their zakat. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And of the livestock, some for carrying and some for flat-lying﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: the hamulah (carrying animals) are the large camels upon which loads are carried, and the farsh (flat-lying animals) are the young ones upon which nothing is carried, taken from spreading (iftirash) over the land with them evenly, like a carpet (farsh). Ibn Bahr said: iftirash is laying them down for slaughter, so the hamulah are the large ones and the farsh are the small ones. The poet said:

He bequeathed to me a hamulah and a farsh, which I stroke (amushshuha) each day with a stroke.

That is, I wipe them. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The second: the hamulah is what is carried upon among the camels and cattle, and the farsh is sheep. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. From this is the saying of Ibn Maslamah:

And we have taken for ourselves the farsh from your livestock, and the hamulat and the mothers of the young.

The third: the hamulah is what carries among camels, cattle, horses, mules, and donkeys, and the farsh is what was created for them from their wool and hides.

﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: from the carrying animals, to clarify that benefiting from their backs does not prevent the permissibility of eating them. The second: it is a permission from Him in general to eat what is lawful from their wealth, and a prohibition against eating what they do not own.

﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: they are his path by which he calls you to disbelief and misguidance. The second: they are his overstepping into declaring the lawful unlawful and the unlawful lawful. We have already mentioned what there is in this of additional interpretation and possibility, and that it is the transition from one sin to another until it encompasses all sins, taken from the step of the foot (khatw al-qadam): its movement from one place to another.

﴿Indeed, he is to you a manifest enemy﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: it is what has become evident to you of his enmity toward your father Adam. The second: what has become evident to you of his enmity toward his allies among the devils, as said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: the trellised ones are those trellised by people, and the untrellised ones are those that grew in the wilderness and the mountains.

Regarding His saying ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ there are three opinions. The first: it is the obligatory charity due on it: a tenth on what is watered without a device, and half a tenth on what is watered with a device. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it is a charity other than the zakat, obligatory on the day of harvest and gathering, and it is feeding those present and leaving what falls from the crop and the fruit. This was said by 'Ata' and Mujahid.

The third: this was obligatory before zakat and then abrogated (naskh) by it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Ibrahim.

﴿And do not be wasteful; indeed, He does not love the wasteful﴾. Concerning this there are five opinions. The first: this forbidden extravagance is that the owner of the property exceeds the amount obligatory upon him to an excess that burdens him. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Jurayj.

Sa'd ibn Sinan narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who exceeds the limit in charity is like the one who withholds it." And it was said: it was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, who gave away all of his produce until nothing remained in it that he could eat.

The second: it is that the ruler takes from him above what is obligatory upon him. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: it is that the owner of the property prevents the giving of the amount obligatory upon him. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The fourth: the intended extravagance is what they used to associate with their idols of tilled land and livestock. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The fifth: it is that one is extravagant in eating from them before paying their zakat. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And of the livestock, some for carrying and some for flat-lying﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: the hamulah (carrying animals) are the large camels upon which loads are carried, and the farsh (flat-lying animals) are the young ones upon which nothing is carried, taken from spreading (iftirash) over the land with them evenly, like a carpet (farsh). Ibn Bahr said: iftirash is laying them down for slaughter, so the hamulah are the large ones and the farsh are the small ones. The poet said:

He bequeathed to me a hamulah and a farsh, which I stroke (amushshuha) each day with a stroke.

That is, I wipe them. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The second: the hamulah is what is carried upon among the camels and cattle, and the farsh is sheep. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. From this is the saying of Ibn Maslamah:

And we have taken for ourselves the farsh from your livestock, and the hamulat and the mothers of the young.

The third: the hamulah is what carries among camels, cattle, horses, mules, and donkeys, and the farsh is what was created for them from their wool and hides.

﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: from the carrying animals, to clarify that benefiting from their backs does not prevent the permissibility of eating them. The second: it is a permission from Him in general to eat what is lawful from their wealth, and a prohibition against eating what they do not own.

﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: they are his path by which he calls you to disbelief and misguidance. The second: they are his overstepping into declaring the lawful unlawful and the unlawful lawful. We have already mentioned what there is in this of additional interpretation and possibility, and that it is the transition from one sin to another until it encompasses all sins, taken from the step of the foot (khatw al-qadam): its movement from one place to another.

﴿Indeed, he is to you a manifest enemy﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: it is what has become evident to you of his enmity toward your father Adam. The second: what has become evident to you of his enmity toward his allies among the devils, as said by al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 143–144:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿eight pairs﴾. As for the zawj (pair, mate), it is a term that applies to the one and to the two. It is said of two that they are a zawj, and it is said of one that it is a zawj, because a thing is not a zawj unless there is with it another that has a name like its name. Labid said:

؎ From every veiled one whose staves are shaded by a pair, upon which are its curtain and its cover

Therefore He said: ﴿eight pairs﴾, because they are eight individuals.

Then He explained them, saying: ﴿of the sheep, two﴾, meaning a male and a female.

(p-181) ﴿And of the goats, two﴾, meaning a male and a female.

﴿Say: Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?﴾ This is a refutation of what the Jahiliyyah had forbidden from them in the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah, the waṣīlah, and the ḥām.

﴿Or what the wombs of the two females contain?﴾ meaning their saying: ﴿What is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾. Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And of the camels, two, and of the cattle, two﴾. He intends by it what He intended with the sheep and the goats, and that these eight pairs are lawful, none of them being forbidden by your prohibition.

Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "this verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when 'Awf ibn Malik came to him and said to him: 'Have you made lawful what our fathers forbade?', meaning of the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah, the waṣīlah, and the ḥām. So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed this verse, saying: ﴿Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?﴾ and 'Awf fell silent because the proof was manifest against him."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 145:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it be carrion﴾. This means that what they (the pagans) had forbidden of the *bahira* (a she-camel whose ears were slit and released, forbidden to be used), the *sa'iba* (a beast released freely for their gods), the *wasila* (a she-camel or ewe that bore twins of the same sex, or a particular offspring), and the *ham* (a stallion camel released after a certain number of covering), God, Exalted is He, did not forbid, nor did He reveal to me its prohibition. Then He specified what is forbidden by way of exception, because the negation of prohibition came in a general form. So He said: ﴿unless it be carrion﴾, which is the animal whose soul has left its body without *dhakat* (the proper ritual slaughter).

﴿or blood poured forth﴾, meaning spilled and flowing. From this, illicit sexual intercourse (*zina*) was called *sifah* (pouring out), because the water (semen) is poured into it and wasted. Tarafa ibn al-Abd said:

"By your grandfather, I did not lampoon you, when the stone idols had blood poured out upon them."

As for blood that is not poured forth: if it is blood in veins that clings to the organ, such as the liver and the spleen, then it is lawful, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood have been made lawful for us. The two kinds of carrion are fish and locusts, and the two kinds of blood are the liver and the spleen." If it is blood that is not in veins clinging to the organ, but is with and within the flesh, then there are two opinions regarding its prohibition. One: it is not forbidden, because the prohibition is restricted to the poured-forth blood. This is the view of ʿA'isha, ʿIkrima, and Qatada. ʿIkrima said: "Were it not for this verse, the Muslims would have searched out the veins of the flesh as the Jews did." The second: it is forbidden, because it is part of the poured-forth blood and a portion of it. The poured-forth blood was mentioned only to exclude the liver and the spleen from it.

﴿or the flesh of swine, for it is impure﴾, meaning filthy and forbidden.

﴿or a deviant offering over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾, meaning what was slaughtered for idols and images. He called it *fisq* (deviance) because it departs from the command of God.

If it is asked: why did He here limit the prohibition to these four, when in surah al-Ma'ida He mentioned others besides them, the strangled (*munkhaniqa*), the beaten to death (*mawquda*), and the fallen (*mutaraddiya*)? The answer: all of these are among the category of carrion, so He mentioned them there in detail, and here in summary.

Regarding this verse there are two opinions. One: it comprises all the forbidden things, so that no animal other than those mentioned in it is forbidden. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿA'isha. The second: it includes the prohibition of what it contains, but it does not encompass all the forbidden things, because the Sunna came with the prohibition of every animal with fangs among beasts of prey and every bird with talons. This is the view of the majority.

(p-182)
(p-183)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 146:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾. This prohibition upon those who were Jews was only a test and a punishment. The first of the things He mentioned as forbidden to them is ﴿every animal with claws﴾, and concerning it there are three opinions. The first: it refers to what does not have divided toes, such as camels, ostriches, geese and ducks. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: it means all kinds of predatory beasts.

The third: it means every animal with a talon among birds, and every animal with a hoof among land animals.

Then He said: ﴿And from the ox and the sheep We forbade them their fat, except what their backs carry﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: it is only the fat of the kidney-enveloping membrane (ath-tharb), said by Qatadah.

The second: it is every fat that is not mixed with bone nor upon bone, said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: it is the fat of the ath-tharb and the kidneys, said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

(p-184) Then He said: ﴿except what their backs carry﴾, meaning the fat of the flank and what clings to the back, for it was not forbidden to them.

Then He said: ﴿or the entrails﴾ (al-hawaya), and concerning it there are four interpretations. The first: they are the intestines (al-mabaʿir), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: they are the milk-vessels (banat al-laban), said by ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

The third: they are the intestines upon which there is fat from their inner side, said by some of the later scholars.

The fourth: they are everything that is coiled in the belly, gathered and curved, said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

﴿or what is mixed with bone﴾: concerning it there are two opinions. One: it is the fat of the flank. The second: it is the fat of the flank and the tail, because it lies upon the coccyx (al-ʿusʿus), said by Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi.

﴿That We repaid them for their rebellion﴾ may bear two meanings. One: for their rebellion against Musa, peace be upon him, in what they demanded and in what they opposed. The second: for their rebellion against themselves in the lawful things which they themselves forbade.

﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ in what He related about them and in what He forbade them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 147–151:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾. This is a command from God to His Prophet ﷺ that he call people to it, so that he may recite to them what God has forbidden them and what He has made lawful for them, in order that they may desist from what the Jahiliyya had been upon, of forbidding what is permitted and permitting what is forbidden.

And al-Tilawa (recitation): it is al-Qira'a (reading). The difference between al-Tilawa and al-Matluw, and between al-Qira'a and al-Maqru', is that al-Tilawa and al-Qira'a are for the first time, while al-Matluw and al-Maqru' are for the second time and beyond. This was mentioned by Ali ibn Isa. What I see as the difference between them is that al-Tilawa and al-Qira'a refer to the utterance, while al-Matluw and al-Maqru' refer to what is uttered.

Then God took a covenant regarding what He forbade, saying: ﴿That you associate nothing with Him﴾. This admits three aspects. One of them: that you do not associate with His worship the worship of another, whether a devil or an idol.

The third: that it carries both matters together.

Then He said: ﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾. Its implied meaning: "And I enjoin upon you good treatment of parents." Good treatment is rendering their rights, avoiding disobedience to them, and guarding their kindness.

﴿And do not kill your children out of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾. This is because they used to kill their children in the Jahiliyya out of fear of poverty.

Regarding al-Imlaq (poverty), there are two opinions: (p-186) One of them: it is al-Iflas (destitution), and from it comes al-Malq (flattery), because it is the effort of the destitute person to draw near to wealth, hoping to postpone it.

The second: al-Imlaq and its meaning are close, although there is a difference between them. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Jurayj.

Then He mentioned the corruption of their belief concerning poverty, saying: ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾, because the provision of all servants, both the guarantor and the guaranteed, rests upon their Creator.

Then He said: ﴿And do not approach the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. One: that this is general to all indecencies, both open and hidden, as said by Qatada.

The second: that it is specific to fornication. What is apparent of them: those who have shops (i.e., prostitutes who are openly displayed); and what is concealed: those who take secret lovers. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi.

The third: what is apparent of them: marrying those who are forbidden; and what is concealed: fornication. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: that what is apparent of them is wine, and what is concealed of them is fornication. This was said by al-Dahhak.

We have also mentioned a fifth possible interpretation: that what is apparent of them is the actions of the limbs, and what is concealed of them is the belief of the hearts.

Then He said: ﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾. The forbidden souls are the soul of a Muslim or a covenanted person. The right by which a soul is killed is what the Prophet ﷺ explained in his saying: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after belief, or fornication after having been married, or killing a soul without a soul." Then He said: ﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you﴾, meaning that God has enjoined His servants with that, and God's injunction is obligatory.

(p-187) Then He said: ﴿That you may understand﴾. This admits two aspects. One: that you understand the prohibition of those matters upon you and know it. The second: that you act as one who understands, which is abandoning what incurs punishment from these forbidden matters.

Then He said: ﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾. The forbidden souls are the soul of a Muslim or a covenanted person. The right by which a soul is killed is what the Prophet ﷺ explained in his saying: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after belief, or fornication after having been married, or killing a soul without a soul." Then He said: ﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you﴾, meaning that God has enjoined His servants with that, and God's injunction is obligatory.

(p-187) Then He said: ﴿That you may understand﴾. This admits two aspects. One: that you understand the prohibition of those matters upon you and know it. The second: that you act as one who understands, which is abandoning what incurs punishment from these forbidden matters.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 147–151:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾. This is a command from God to His Prophet ﷺ that he call people to it, so that he may recite to them what God has forbidden them and what He has made lawful for them, in order that they may desist from what the Jahiliyya had been upon, of forbidding what is permitted and permitting what is forbidden.

And al-Tilawa (recitation): it is al-Qira'a (reading). The difference between al-Tilawa and al-Matluw, and between al-Qira'a and al-Maqru', is that al-Tilawa and al-Qira'a are for the first time, while al-Matluw and al-Maqru' are for the second time and beyond. This was mentioned by Ali ibn Isa. What I see as the difference between them is that al-Tilawa and al-Qira'a refer to the utterance, while al-Matluw and al-Maqru' refer to what is uttered.

Then God took a covenant regarding what He forbade, saying: ﴿That you associate nothing with Him﴾. This admits three aspects. One of them: that you do not associate with His worship the worship of another, whether a devil or an idol.

The third: that it carries both matters together.

Then He said: ﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾. Its implied meaning: "And I enjoin upon you good treatment of parents." Good treatment is rendering their rights, avoiding disobedience to them, and guarding their kindness.

﴿And do not kill your children out of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾. This is because they used to kill their children in the Jahiliyya out of fear of poverty.

Regarding al-Imlaq (poverty), there are two opinions: (p-186) One of them: it is al-Iflas (destitution), and from it comes al-Malq (flattery), because it is the effort of the destitute person to draw near to wealth, hoping to postpone it.

The second: al-Imlaq and its meaning are close, although there is a difference between them. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Jurayj.

Then He mentioned the corruption of their belief concerning poverty, saying: ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾, because the provision of all servants, both the guarantor and the guaranteed, rests upon their Creator.

Then He said: ﴿And do not approach the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. One: that this is general to all indecencies, both open and hidden, as said by Qatada.

The second: that it is specific to fornication. What is apparent of them: those who have shops (i.e., prostitutes who are openly displayed); and what is concealed: those who take secret lovers. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi.

The third: what is apparent of them: marrying those who are forbidden; and what is concealed: fornication. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: that what is apparent of them is wine, and what is concealed of them is fornication. This was said by al-Dahhak.

We have also mentioned a fifth possible interpretation: that what is apparent of them is the actions of the limbs, and what is concealed of them is the belief of the hearts.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 152–153:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾. He singled out the property of the orphan for mention, although the property of others is equally forbidden to take, because greed for it is stronger given the scarcity of those who look after it, so mentioning it was more fitting.

Concerning His saying ﴿except in the way that is best﴾ there are four interpretations. The first: preserving his property for him until he grows up so that he may take possession of it; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: that it means trading with it; this was said by Mujahid.

The third: that it means not taking any of the profit when one trades with the property on his behalf; this was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: that the guardian may eat from his property in a reasonable manner if he is poor, and abstain if he is rich, and not go beyond eating to clothing or anything else; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

It may also admit a fifth: that "the way that is best" means preserving its principal and developing its yield.

Then He said ﴿until he reaches his maturity (ashudd)﴾. Al-Ashudd means strength and youth.

Concerning its definition there are three sayings: (p-188) The first: that it is puberty, at which point good deeds and bad deeds are recorded for him; this was said by Rabi'ah, Zayd ibn Aslam and Malik.

The second: that al-Ashudd is thirty years; this was said by al-Suddi.

The third: that al-Ashudd is eighteen years; this was mentioned by Ali ibn Isa, and there are other aspects which we will mention later.

Then the Exalted said ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice﴾, meaning with justice. He was commanded regarding the property of the seller to render it in the same manner as he was commanded regarding the property of the orphan.

Then He said ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, meaning: since justice in weighing and measuring is required, and fixing the smallest of small amounts is impossible, that is pardoned, because it does not fall within capacity, so He did not impose it.

Then He said ﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative﴾. It may carry three meanings: The first: when you judge, then be equitable. The second: when you testify, then be truthful. The third: when you mediate, then do not lean (to one side).

Then He said ﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾. Concerning it there are two sayings: The first: that the covenant of Allah is everything a person has obligated upon himself, such as a vow and other things. The second: that it is an oath by Allah, that fulfilling it is binding unless it involves disobedience.

﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may remember﴾. Concerning it there are two aspects: The first: that it refers to those who were Jews and what He enjoined upon them in the Torah. The second: that it refers to the Muslims and what He enjoined upon them in the Qur'an.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And that this is My path, which is straight, so follow it﴾. Concerning it there are two sayings: The first: that it is the Qur'an. The second: that it is the Shari'ah (the revealed law), and that was called a path (sirat), and the sirat is the road, because it leads to Paradise, so it became a road to it.

﴿So follow it﴾, meaning in acting upon it.

(p-189) ﴿And do not follow other ways﴾. Concerning it there are three aspects: The first: the earlier revealed scriptures, which it abrogated by the Qur'an, and this is a possibility. The second: the earlier religions, which it abrogated by Islam, and this is a possibility. The third: innovations (bid'ah) and doubtful matters (shubuhat).

﴿Lest you be scattered away from His path﴾, meaning away from the road of His religion.

It may also admit a second aspect: that His path is the support of His religion and jihad against its enemies, so He forbade division and commanded unity.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 154–155:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book, complete, upon the one who did good﴾. Regarding His saying ﴿complete upon the one who did good﴾, there are five opinions.

The first: complete upon Moses' goodness in obeying Him. This was said by al-Rabi' and al-Farra' (al-Farra', a grammarian and Qur'an scholar).

The second: complete upon the doers of good (muhsinin). This was said by Mujahid. Ibn Mas'ud used to recite: (complete upon those who did good, alladhina ahsanu).

The third: complete upon God's goodness to His prophets. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: complete for his honor in Paradise upon his goodness in this world. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatada.

The fifth: complete for the blessing of God upon Abraham, because he was of his offspring. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The third: complete upon God's goodness to His prophets. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: complete for his honor in Paradise upon his goodness in this world. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatada.

The fifth: complete for the blessing of God upon Abraham, because he was of his offspring. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on surah 6, verses 156–158:**

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them﴾. There are two interpretations. The first: "Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them as messengers?" meaning the disbelievers who hold back from faith although the proofs have become manifest.

The second: "Do they await, meaning, regarding the proofs and signs of God, anything but that the angels should come to them to seize their souls?" This was said by Juwaybir.

﴿Or your Lord should come﴾. There are two interpretations. The first: the command of your Lord regarding the punishment, said by al-Hasan.

The second: the decree of your Lord on the Day of Resurrection, said by Mujahid.

﴿Or some of the signs of your Lord should come﴾. There are two views. The first: it is the rising of the sun from its west, said by Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi. Ibn Mas'ud said: "together with the moon at one time," and he recited: ﴿and the sun and the moon are joined together﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:9].

The second: the rising of the sun from its west, the Dajjal (the Antichrist), and the beast of the earth, said by Abu Hurayra.

(p-191) ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾: regarding the first and last of the signs of the Hour there are two views. The first: the first of them is the Dajjal, then the smoke, then Yajuj and Majuj (Gog and Magog), then the beast, then the rising of the sun from its west, ﴿when faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before﴾. This is the view of Mu'adh ibn Jabal.

The second: the first of them is the emergence of the Dajjal, then the emergence of Yajuj and Majuj, then the rising of the sun from its west, ﴿when faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before﴾, then the emergence of the beast. This is the view of Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, and he transmitted it as marfu' (traced directly to the Prophet).

Then they differed as to whether faith ceases to benefit a soul at the appearance of the first sign or at the appearance of the last of them, on two views. The first: when the first sign emerges, the pens are cast aside, the recording angels sit down, and the bodies testify concerning the deeds.

The second view: that happens with the emergence of the last of the signs, so that there may remain for us an effect in warning.

Then He said: ﴿or has earned good through its faith﴾. As for faith before these signs, it is counted. As for faith after them, if the soul has not earned good in it, it is not counted; and if it has earned good in it, then regarding whether it is counted there are two views. The first: it is counted, and this is the apparent meaning of the verse, whether it was before the signs or after them.

The second: it is not counted, and its meaning is: it did not believe before and it earned good in its faith. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Regarding the good that is earned, there are two views. The first: performing the obligatory duties in their most complete condition.

The second: voluntary acts of worship (nawafil) beyond the obligatory duties.

(p-192) Mujahid narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The door of repentance is open from the direction of the west. Repentance is accepted except from three: from Iblis, the head of disbelief; from Qabil, the killer of Habil; and from one who kills a prophet, for him there is no repentance. When the sun rises from that door like a black sediment, having no light, until it reaches the middle of the sky and then turns back, the door will be closed and repentance will be rejected, so that faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before, or that earned good in its faith. Then it returns to its rising-places, and it rises after that a hundred and twenty years later, except that these are years that pass swiftly."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects﴾. Regarding who they are, there are four opinions. The first: they are the Jews specifically, as said by Mujahid. The second: they are the Jews and the Christians, as said by Qatadah. The third: they are all the polytheists, as said by al-Hasan. The fourth: they are the people of misguidance from this community, as said by Abu Hurayrah.

Regarding the division they made, there are two views. The first: it is the religion that God commanded, which they divided by disagreeing about it and following doubtful matters (shubuhat). The second: it is the disbelief that they held as their religion.

The meaning of His words ﴿and became sects﴾ is that they became groups (firaq).

It may also carry another sense: that the sects (shiya', plural of shi'ah, "party") are those who are united in supporting one another, and this is the more likely, because they unite behind one matter despite disagreeing about others.

[p-193] Regarding its root, there are two views. The first: its root is "to become apparent," from the saying "the news spread (shaa'a al-khabar)" when it became known. The second: its root is "to follow," from the saying "he supported him in the matter (shaayaḥahu 'ala al-amr)" when he followed him. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You have nothing to do with them in anything﴾. Regarding this, there are two views. The first: you have nothing to do with fighting them, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by Surat al-Tawbah, as said by al-Kalbi. The second: you have nothing to do with mixing with them, which is a prohibition to His Prophet (ﷺ) from drawing near to them and a command to him to keep away from them, as said by Qatadah, just as al-Nabighah said:

"When she attempts wickedness against Asad, I am not of you, and you are not of me."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 160:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is ten times its like, and whoever comes with an evil deed, he will not be recompensed except with its like﴾. Regarding "good deed" (al-hasanah) and "evil deed" (al-sayyi'ah) here, there are two opinions. The first: the good deed is faith (iman) and the evil deed is disbelief (kufr). This was said by Abu Salih.

The second: it is general, concerning good deeds and evil deeds, in that He made the recompense for a good deed ten times its like as an act of grace (tafaddul), and made the recompense for an evil deed its like as an act of justice ('adl). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah distance from Himself the one whose single (sin) overcomes ten (good deeds)." Then, concerning this, there are two opinions. The first: it is general for all people.

The second: it is specific to the Bedouin (al-a'rab), that when one of them comes with a good deed, for him is ten times its like. As for others among the emigrants (al-muhajirin), for whoever of them comes with a good deed, (the reward is) seven hundred. This was said by Ibn 'Umar and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

As for the multiplication of a good deed by ten times its like, it is because Allah made obligatory the tenth of their wealth, and they used to fast three days in every month, which are the "white days" (al-bid) of it. So the last tenth of the wealth was the last of all their wealth, and the last of the three days was the last of the whole month.

As for multiplying that by seven hundred fold, it is due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whomever He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. So Allah multiplied the good deed by seven hundred fold. Al-Hasan al-Basri used to recite ﴿fa-lahu ʿashru amthalihā﴾ with tanwin (fa-lahu ʿashrun amthāluhā), and its grammatical basis (wajh) in Arabic is sound.

Ibn Bahr related in the verse an interpretation that departs from the apparent generality, which is that "good deed" is a general noun applied to every type of faith, and it is applied according to its generality. If "good deed" is applied to one single type of it, then for it there is no reward except one like; and if it is applied to a good deed comprising two types, the reward for it is two likes, as in His saying: ﴿Fear Allah and believe in His Messenger, He will give you a double portion (kiflayn) of His mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 28]. The kifl is the portion, like the like (mithl). So He made for those who feared Allah and believed in the Messenger two portions: a portion for the fear of Allah, and a portion for their belief in His Messenger. This indicates that the good deed for which ten likes are given is that which gathers ten types of good deeds, and it is the faith which Allah gathered in its description into ten types by His saying: ﴿Indeed the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women…﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and a great reward﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35]. These ten types are those whose reward is ten times their like, so each type has one like. This interpretation is corrupt, because it departs from the apparent generality, by what the specification of the general does not bear. For what gathers ten types is ten good deeds, and so it recompenses only its like for a good deed, and it becomes invalid that the recompense for a good deed is ten times its like.

Some of the exegetes mentioned a third interpretation: that for it is ten times its like in bliss and increase, not in great rank, because the rank of honour is attained only through obedience, and this is a multiplication of grace, as He said: ﴿That He may pay them their wages in full and increase them of His bounty﴾ [Fatir: 30].

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verses 161–163:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ This is a command from Allah Most High to His Prophet (ﷺ) that he should tell the people about the state of his worship and to whom belongs the command in his life and in his death.

He said ﴿Indeed, my prayer﴾, which is the prescribed prayer, with bowing and prostration, comprising humility and submission to Allah Most High alone, to the exclusion of an idol or a human being.

Then He said: ﴿and my sacrifice (nusuk)﴾. Regarding it here there are three opinions. The first: it is the sacrificial animal slaughtered in the Hajj and the 'Umrah. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak.

The second: its meaning is my religion. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: its meaning is my worship. This was said by al-Zajjaj, from the saying of people, "So-and-so is a nasik," meaning a worshipper. The difference between religion (din) and worship ('ibadah) is that religion is belief (i'tiqad), while worship is action ('amal).

The words of the Most High: ﴿and my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ admit of two meanings. The first: his life and his death are in the hand of Allah Most High; no one other than Him possesses for him life or death. Therefore he was (a worshipper) praying and performing rites for Him.

The second: his life is for Allah in that it is devoted to His obedience, and his death is for Him in his return to His recompense.

I have found in it a third meaning: my deeds in my life and my bequest at the time of my death are for Allah.

Then He said: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, an attribute of Allah Most High, that He is the Owner of the worlds to the exclusion of others; therefore He is more worthy of obedience and worship than anyone else.

Then Allah Most High said: ﴿He has no partner﴾, which admits of two meanings. The first: He has no partner in the dominion of the worlds.

The second: He has no partner in worship.

(p-196) ﴿And of that I have been commanded﴾, meaning what has been mentioned above.

﴿And I am the first of the Muslims﴾, meaning first of this Ummah, as an exhortation to follow him and to hasten to Islam.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 6, verse 164:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Say: Shall I seek a lord other than Allah, when He is the Lord of everything?﴾ The occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers of Quraysh invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the religion of his forefathers, in worshipping al-Lat and al-Uzza, and they said: "O Muhammad, if it is a burden (wizr), then it is upon us, not upon you." So this verse was revealed to him.

﴿And no soul earns [sin] except against itself﴾, meaning: upon it is the punishment for its disobedience, and for it is the reward for its obedience.

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, that is, no one bears the sin of another so that he becomes sinful because of it and is punished for it, nor does one carry the sin of another so that he is cleared of it and safe from its punishment.

Regarding the original meaning of wizr there are two views. The first: its origin is heaviness, from His saying: ﴿And We removed from you your burden, which had weighed upon your back﴾ [al-Sharh: 2–3]. From this the minister of a king (wazir) is named, because he bears the heaviness on his behalf.

The second: its origin is refuge, from His saying: ﴿No! There is no refuge (wazar)﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11]. From this the minister of a king is also named, because he is turned to (taken as a refuge) in matters.

The second view: each era succeeds the era before it. Whenever one generation passes, another generation follows it in an orderly fashion, until the Hour arrives upon the final generation, and no further generation is created. Thus this community became successors (khalaf) to the earlier nations.

The third view: He made some of them successors to others, so that they might be united through mutual cooperation.

The fourth view: because they are the last of the nations, and they were successors to those who came before them. Al-Shammakh said:

They strike you and miss me, the fates, and I am left behind in the abodes, after the abodes [of others].

﴿And He raised some of you above others in degrees﴾, meaning He differentiated among them in wealth, nobility of lineage, and physical strength. This, though He initiated it as an act of grace without recompense or entitlement, contains, by His judgment, encouragement toward what is above and warning against what is below, so that desire and fear may endure for Him.

He drew attention to this by His saying: ﴿that He may test you in what He has given you﴾, meaning of wealth and strength. In this there are two views. The first: that He may test you by gratitude (i'tiraf).

﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾. If it is asked: how did He make it swift when it is in the Hereafter?

There are three answers to this. The first: every thing that is coming is near, as in His saying: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or it is nearer﴾ [al-Nahl: 77]. The second: your Lord is swift in punishment in this world for whoever deserves having his punishment hastened in it.

The third: that when He wills to punish, He punishes, so His punishment is swift because it is conjoined with His will. This is the saying of Ibn Bahr.

﴿And indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, combining what entails fear, through the swiftness of punishment, with what entails desire, through forgiveness and mercy, because combining desire and fear is more effective in compliance with obedience and in refraining from disobedience. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows best.
